input: Given question: 13 year old Brian is brought to clinic. He has Prader-Willi Syndrome, and suffers with behavioral problems, obesity, hyperphagia, and learning disabilities as a result of this. Which of the following deletions has caused Brian's Prader-Willi Syndrome? Option A: 5p deletion Option B: 22q11.2 deletion Option C: 4p deletion Option D: 15q11-q13 deletion Option E: 17p11.2 deletion The correct answer is Option D.
reference: 15q11-q13 deletion = Prader-Willi Syndrome 22q11.2 deletion = DiGeorge Syndrome/Velocardiofacial Syndrome 5p deletion = Fragile X Syndrome 4p deletion = Smith-Magenis Syndrome 17p11.2 deletion = Angelman Syndrome Deletions in the 16th chromosome can cause Klinefleter syndrome, which affects males and causes hypogonadism, primary amenorrhea, and small genitalia. Also affects renal development, so they have small kidneys. They are diagnosed via karyotyping. MonosomyX (45, X0) can also occur, which results in sex reversal. This can be diagnosed pre-natally via chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis. Trisomy 8 occurs in Patau syndrome. This can be detected via karyotype analysis of peripheral blood or tissue culture. I hope this helps! References:https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/prader-willi-syndrome/https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/angeilman-syndrome/https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/diageorge-syndrome/https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/smith-magenis-syndrome/https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fragile-x/related-conditions/klinefelter-syndrome/https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/monosomy-x/https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/trisomy-8/https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/trisomy-18/ Reference link: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vucardiofacialsyndrome/ (this website has been used as a reference throughout) All information has been taken from this website, which provides an excellent overview of all of these syndromes. It is recommended that you read through this website thoroughly to get a good understanding of each condition. If you want to know more about any specific condition, just click on it! There is also loads of info about genetic counselling and testing, including prenatal testing. If you have any questions, ask your healthcare professional!
best_explanation: D - correct, this deletion causes PWS. It is the most common deletion to cause PWS.  A - this deletion causes Angelman Syndrome.  B - this deletion causes DiGeorge Syndrome.  C - this deletion causes Smith-Magenis Syndrome.  E - this deletion causes Börjeson-Forssman-Lehman Syndrome. 15q11-q13 deletion causes PWS, and is the most common deletion to cause this condition. It is inherited in an imprinted manner, meaning that if one parent passes on the deleted chromosome 15, their child will have PWS. The same parent will also have the traits of PWS, but they will not have the syndrome itself. If the other parent passes on the deleted chromosome 15, their child will not have PWS. However, they may have the traits of the syndrome, as it is inherited in an imprinted manner. Parents who have a child with PWS have a 25% chance of having another child with PWS, and a 50% chance of being a carrier. Children of affected individuals have a 50% chance of inheriting the deleted chromosome 15, and therefore PWS. input: Given question: A 10-year old girl with an autosomal dominant mutation in sarcomeric protein is being evaluated by a pediatric cardiologist. The family history reveals that the patient's father died suddenly at age 33 while running Cardiff half-marathon. What was the likely finding on histological evaluation of his father's heart at autopsy? Option A: Myocyte disarray, which suggests Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) Option B: Amyloid deposits, indicative of Restrictive Cardiomyopathy Option C: Wavy myocytes, which suggests Myocardial Infarction Option D: Viral particles - Coxsackievirus, indicative of Dilated Cardiomyopathy Option E: Eosinophilic infiltration deposits, indicative of Restrictive Cardiomyopathy The correct answer is Option A.
reference: Autosomal dominant mutation in sarcomeric protein = HCM A = Correct. HCM is characterized by uncoordinated contraction of myocytes, resulting in a 'disarrayed' appearance. It is the most common genetic cause of HCM and has been identified in many proteins that form part of the sarcomere, including titin, alpha-actin, and myosin binding protein C. HCM is associated with sudden death in young people. B = Incorrect. Restrictive Cardiomyopathy is characterized by infiltrative fibrosis of the myocardium. This leads to decreased ventricular distensibility and impaired ventricular filling. C = Incorrect. Wavy myocytes are characteristic of hypertrophy due to increased workload, such as in Pressure Overload Cardiomyopathy. D = Incorrect. Although viral particles may be present, they would not be diagnostic of DCM. There are no specific pathognomonic histological findings for any type of cardiomyopathy. E = Incorrect. Eosinophilic infiltration deposits are characteristic of allergic angioedema. Allergic angioedema is a type of Brunsting-Perry disease. It is not related to cardiomyopathies. REF: Dr Yousef Zaheer's Lecture; Case 16. Medicine Park, Australian Capital Territory, Australia.
best_explanation: The answer is A.  This patient has an autosomal dominant mutation in sarcomeric protein, which suggests a diagnosis of HCM. Her father likely had the same mutation and died suddenly while running due to a cardiac arrest. The most likely finding on histological evaluation of his heart at autopsy would be myocyte disarray, which is characteristic of HCM. B: Amyloid deposits are characteristic of Restrictive Cardiomyopathy, but this patient has an autosomal dominant mutation in sarcomeric protein, which suggests a diagnosis of HCM.C: Wavy myocytes are seen in patients with hypertension, but this patient has an autosomal dominant mutation in sarcomeric protein, which suggests a diagnosis of HCM.D: Viral particles - Coxsackievirus are characteristic of dilated cardiomyopathy, but this patient has an autosomal dominant mutation in sarcomeric protein, which suggests a diagnosis of HCM.E: Eosinophilic infiltration deposits are characteristic of Restrictive Cardiomyopathy, but this patient has an autosomal dominant mutation in sarcomeric protein, which suggests a diagnosis of HCM. Link to case 12 wrap up. https://www.cardiff.ac.uk/news/articles/2021/03/case-12-wrap-up.html  Dr Yousef's lecture on cardiomyopathies. input: Given question: A 13-year-old boy presents to his GP with anxiety. After some time, he admits that he is embarrassed about his body; he is much taller and lankier than all of his brothers, has some breast development, and has a small penis and testicles. The GP reviews his notes and sees that he was previously diagnosed with mild dyslexia. A blood test shows that he has low testosterone, and subsequent genetic testing reveals an abnormality in chromosome 23. What is the likely karyotype of his chromosome 23? Option A: YYY, Delilah Option B: 45, Y Option C: 47, XXY Option D: 47, XYY Option E: 48, XXYY The correct answer is Option C.
reference: This patient has Klinefelter's syndrome, which typically presents as primary hypogonadism (small testes/testosterone), gynecomastia, and pubertal gynaecomastia. There are often cognitive and behavioural problems, including learning difficulties and social withdrawal. These symptoms could be confused with those of other neurodevelopmental conditions, such as ADHD or autism spectrum disorder. Klinefelter's syndrome occurs in approximately 1 in 600 males and results from an extra X chromosome (XXY). The most common cause of primary hypogonadism is a microdeletion at the CFTR gene on chromosome 1. This cause was excluded in this patient due to normal intelligence and lack of physical signs of cystic fibrosis. The other options listed are other forms of chromosomal variation. Case 7 - Dr Alex Murray - Chromosomal Abnormalities Lecture - slides 27-30. I have also included a link to an NHS website article about Klinefelter's syndrome: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/klinefelters-syndrome/introduction/
best_explanation: The answer is C; he has Klinefelter's syndrome, which typically presents as primary hypogonadism (low testosterone), pubertal gynaecomastia and small testes and penis. About 1 in 1000 men have this syndrome. There are many other symptoms that can occur, depending on the severity of the condition, including tall stature, breast development, infertility and learning disabilities. Klinefelter's syndrome results from an extra X chromosome, usually XXY. Source: 'Human Dysmorphology' lecture in Case 7, and 'Endocrine Anatomy and Physiology of the Reproductive System' lecture in Case 12.  Delilah is a character in the Bible who was paid to entice Samson (from the book of Judges) with her hair, and is often depicted as a temptress. YYY and 45 are both normal karyotypes. 47, XXY is the karyotype of Klinefelter's syndrome, as mentioned above.  47, XYY is the karyotype of a condition called 'XXYY syndrome'. This is much rarer than Klinefelter's syndrome, and typically results in tall stature, severe learning disabilities, and a lack of social and emotional development. Source: 'Human Dysmorphology' lecture in Case 7.  'A' is a made up, and 'B' and 'D' are normal karyotypes. 'E' is the karyotype of a form of down syndrome called 'mosaic down syndrome'. In this condition, some cells have an extra copy of chromosome 21, whereas others do not. This means that some people with mosaic down syndrome have fewer symptoms than people with trisomy 21 (the most common form of down syndrome). Source: 'Human Dysmorphology' lecture in Case 7.

input: Given question: A 27-year-old woman presents with amenorrhoea, and a subsequent pregnancy test gives a positive result. She takes a lithium-based drug to treat her schizophrenia; lithium is known to have teratogenic effects such as inhibiting the formation of new blood vessels from endothelial cells in the embryo. Which process, described above, is inhibited by lithium? Option A: Angiogenesis Option B: Arborisation Option C: Haematopoiesis Option D: Somatogenesis Option E: Vasculogenesis The correct answer is Option E.
reference: Angio - formation of new blood vessels (from endothelial cells) Arborisation - formation of small capillaries that allow nutrients to diffuse into tissues Haematopoiesis - production of blood cells Somatogenesis - formation of body structures Vasculogenesis - formation of the vasculature during embryonic development Lithium inhibits vasculogenesis, which is the formation of the vasculature during embryonic development. This means that as the embryo does not have a fully developed vascular system, it is unable to receive nutrition and oxygen, resulting in death or severe malformations. Schizophrenia drugs - lithium, clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone, aripiprazole Case 7 lecture Dr Lisa Wallace TJ's comments:the other choices are processes related to the formation of blood vessels, arteries and capillaries, which allows haemotological tissue to survive. Note that angiogenesis is the process of forming new blood vessels from endothelial cells. The others are all different ways of describing the same process.vasculogenesis is the formation of the vasculature during embryonic development, so this is what would be inhibited by lithium. From the case 16 lecture on teratology. Other drugs that are known to cause birth defects include:• corticosteroids • antiepileptics • mood stabilizers (e.g. valproate, lithium)• antipsychotics • immunosuppressants• chemotherapy• HIV drugs• weight loss drugs• thyroid medication• NSAIDs• diabetes drugs• fertility drugs• miscellaneous other drugs For more information see the patient.co.uk website. Also, Dr Wallace mentioned that a lot of drugs taken during pregnancy have no data on their safety in humans because of ethical reasons, so we have to rely on animal studies and pharmacokinetic modelling. TJ's further comments:it is important to note that some of these drugs do have teratogenic effects but only at high doses. E.g. corticosteroids, antiepileptics, mood stabilisers, antipsychotics, NSAIDs. Others have a higher risk at any dose e.g. chemotherapy, HIV drugs, weight loss drugs, diabetes drugs, miscellaneous other drugs. Most drugs taken during pregnancy fall into the first category, i.e. they have a teratogenic effect only at high doses. There is no recommended daily allowance for drugs during pregnancy, it is just generally acknowledged that they should be avoided where possible. A lot of drugs are excreted in breastmilk, so if a mother takes a drug and has a child with special needs, it is hard to work out whether the drug was responsible or whether there were other factors. In terms of schemes, the best one to use is probably SNOMED CT because it is very comprehensive and includes lots of synonyms, so you are more likely to find the term you are looking for. You can also use external links to take you to pages about specific drugs and their effects on foetal development. Taken from Case 7 lecture Dr Lisa Wallace plenary on schizophrenia drugs. Her slides can be found here: https://www.dropbox.com/sh/5a4st8m4emxv7c07/AAAHqOY8S9V6b7u3_EgRnGta?dl=0
best_explanation: From Coffey lecture in case 7.  Lithium inhibits vasculogenesis, the process of creating new blood vessels from endothelial cells. This has implications in the development of the embryo, as without this process the embryo will not be able to obtain the necessary nutrients to grow.  Angiogenesis - the formation of new blood vessels from pre-existing vessels. Arborisation - the process of branching of blood vessels to reach all parts of an organ. Haematopoiesis - the process of blood cell formation, including erythrocytes (red blood cells), leukocytes (white blood cells), and thrombocytes (platelets). Somatogenesis - the process of the development of the body from the egg until the end of the fetal period.  Reference: Coffey Lecture, Case 7, Teratology.  Further details can be found in Dave Wilson's lecture on Congenital Malformations and Teratology, as well as in the textbook 'Teratology' by Moore and Persaud. input: Given question: A 28 year old male is brought into A&E due to muscle rigidity and drowsiness. He has a history of schizophrenia and is taking Clozapine. Doctors diagnosed with Neuroleptic Malignancy Syndrome. If his history was not clear (i.e the history of schizophrenia was unknown, no drug history) what feature would help you diagnose NMS rather than Serotonin Syndrome? Option A: decreased reflexes Option B: increased reflexes Option C: tachycardia Option D: pyrexia Option E: dilated pupils The correct answer is Option A.
reference: Features of serotonin syndrome: * Increased reflexes ** Hyperreflexia ** Tachycardia *** Fever *** Vomiting**** Diarrhoea **** Muscle clonus ***** Bradycardia ***** Hyporeflexia Features of neuroleptic malignancy syndrome: * Decreased reflexes * Rigidity * Tachycardia * Fever * Vomiting * Leucopenia * Eosinophilia * High CPK levels * No overt psychosis or aggression NMS is an idiosyncratic reaction, patients may be on multiple medications so it is essential to ask about other meds as well as alcohol intake. NMS more likely in first few months of treatment, higher incidence in females and in the elderly. Serotonin syndrome can occur at any time, even after many years of treatment, and has no age, sex or race predilection. Treatment: for both - cooling measures, fluids, antiemetics, sedation, and sometimes adrenaline/noradrenaline for extreme hyperreflexia. for NMS - Citalopram (SSRI) for 7 days, if this doesn't work then switch to Phenelzine (MAOI). if these don't work then plenary neurolgical intervention including muscle relaxants, benzodiazepines, and occasionally therapeutic hypothermia. For Serotonin syndrome - IV cyclizine, diphenhydramine, lorazepam, and metoclopramide. Agitation may be treated with IM lorazepam. If patient teeters into serotonin syndrome from NMS, treat as above, however if patient develops neurontin malignancy syndrome from the treatment of serotonin syndrome then this could potentially result in death. input: Given question: A 28-year old women presents to A&E after she fainted on the way to her car after work: you see she is struggling to breath and she admits to SOB and tiredness for the last few weeks. She was diagnosed Crohn's disease 8 years ago. She recently had a stomach bug, causing her to vomit several times a day. You notice a nasty abrasion on the palm of her hand where she fell, which is oozing blood and looks dirty. You do some tests... Haemoglobin: 98 g/L (115-165)Ferritin: 20 ng/mL (12-150)Folate: 4.8 ng/mL (>4)B12: 140 pg/ML (180-1000)MCV: 103 fL (80-100)  Her O2 sats on air are 93%. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment Option A: B12 injection Option B: clean and dress the wound, give a tetanus booster Option C: cross-matched blood transfusion Option D: high-flow oxygen Option E: IV iron-transfusion The correct answer is Option D.
reference: This patient has Fe deficiency Anaemia (98g/L), which is caused by chronic bleeding due to her Crohn's (the reason she is struggling to breathe). We need to treat the cause of the bleeding (wounded duodenum), then treat the anaemia with IV iron. B12 and Folate are also low, but iron deficiency anaemia takes priority. Give high-flow oxygen to raise her sats. A - B12 injections are only given to treat Vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia, which this patient does not have. B - It is important to clean and dress the wound, however giving a tetanus booster is not necessary at this point as she has no sign of infection (swelling, redness or heat) and it is more important to treat the anaemia C - Cross-matched blood transfusions are used to treat sensitivity to antibodies in donor blood. This patient hasn't been diagnosed with any coeliac or diabetes so wouldn't need this treatment. D - Correct, treat the anaemia first e.g. with intravenous ferric sulphate. E - IV iron-transfusion is only needed if oral iron cannot be tolerated, there is a contraindication to oral iron or the patient needs immediate correction of their anaemia. In this case, oral iron will suffice. *It is also important to investigate why she has Crohn's, but that is beyond the scope of this question.* References: 'Haemotological aspects of Crohn's disease' lecture, Case 11. 'NICE Guidelines: Iron Deficiency Anaemia' (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg32ndelivery/iron-deficiency-anaemia#initiative=view%3A/guidelines/cg32/delivery/iron-deficiency-anaemia%3Anice-guideline) 'Blood Transfusion' lecture, Case 12. 'When to use parenteral iron therapy' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3973275/) 'Oxygen Therapy' lecture, Case 10. 'An introduction to oxygen delivery' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK538475/)
best_explanation: This patient has Crohn's disease and is suffering from a flare-up, causing her to be tired and short of breath. She has lost a lot of blood and is therefore anaemic. She is also suffering from malnutrition due to her Crohn's and recent stomach bug. She is now developing septic shock due to the infection from her wound. She needs high-flow oxygen in order to increase her oxygenation and therefore save her life. B12 and iron infusions would be useful, but are not emergency life-saving treatments. Giving her blood would be very risky, as she may be rhesus negative and the transfusion could cause haemolytic transfusion reaction. IV iron would also not help her condition immediately. This is a classic example of when the primary survey is completed and the patient is still unstable, you would prioritise the airway, breathing and circulation. This patient is clearly struggling to breath, so oxygen is the first priority, followed by ensuring the patient is ventilating effectively and finally, looking after the circulation. input: Given question: A 33 year old male says he finds no pleasure in life and is always tired. He can sometimes hear voices and thinks everyone around him is part of a conspiracy theory. He is admitted to an acute psychiatric ward and given a conventional anti-psychotic. His hallucinations and paranoia improve but now complains he has a tremor and cannot move about quickly. He is switched to another drug which resolves this but requires blood monitoring. What is thhe anti-psychotic he is now on? Option A: Haloperidol Option B: Chlorpromazine Option C: Clozapine Option D: Fluoxetine Option E: Benzodiazepine The correct answer is Option C.
reference: C - Correct answer! This patient is experiencing extra-pyramidal side effects (EPS) so his anti-psychotic is changed to clozapine which is an atypical anti-psychotic. It targets serotonin and dopamine receptors. It is associated with agranulocytosis and hence requires regular blood tests to check WBC. reference: AS is a Seronegative Arthropathy - meaning it is not associated with any bacteria so cannot be caught from someone else. It mainly affects young males and the symptoms are: Morning stiffness which lasts more than 30 minutes, Pain which is relieved by exercise but worsens at night, Inter scapular muscle spasms, Loss of movement in the spine (asthmatic component) There is no conclusive test for AS but the following may suggest it: Inflammatory markers in blood, XR of the affected joint, MRI of the affected area. The condition used to be called "kyphoscoliosis" but this is now considered a result of AS.  Quada Equina Syndrome is characterised by: Lower back/gluteal pain which radiates into the leg below the knee, Pain is usually aggravated by walking and relieved by sitting down, Muscle wastage, Weakness and deformation of the spine (kyphoscoliosis). This condition is caused by damage to nerve roots in the spine resulting in loss of communication between the brain and the nerves that control the muscles in the lower part of the body.  Spondylosis is when there is generalised wear and tear on the spine, discs and adjacent soft tissues. It often occurs due to degenerative disc disease. Symptoms include: Chronic lower back pain, Stiffness in the morning which lasts less than 30 minutes, Pain which is relieved by exercise but worsens at night.  Spondylolisthesis is a defect or stress fracture of the pars interarticularis. This causes a forward displacement of one vertebrae brke relative to another. Symptoms include: Chronic lower back pain which is worse at night, Pain which is relieved by exercise.  Herniation of intervertebral disk cause pressure on the surrounding nerve root(s). Symptoms include: Radiating pain, Paresthesia, Muscle weakness.  For more info see Prof Alan Gross's lecture on Spinal Diseases in Case 12. input: Given question: A 42 year old woman presents to her local GP after performing a home pregnancy test with a positive result. Her last menstrual period was 14 weeks ago and she has a BMI of 29kg/m2. The GP recommends that she has a screening test for Down's syndrome. Betty expresses her concern about the accuracy of the test, having had a friend who had a false positive result. Which screening test would be most appropriate? Option A: Amniocentesis Option B: Chorionic Villus Sampling Option C: Combined Test Option D: NIFTY Option E: Quadruple Test The correct answer is Option E.
reference:
The combined test is not appropriate as it is too late in pregnancy (>15 weeks) and also involves ultrasound which is not suitable at 14 weeks. Amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling are both diagnostic testing as they both require removal of tissue from the fetus or placenta and are therefore far too expensive and invasive for routine screening in pregnancies without risk factors. The NIFTY test is a blood test that assesses levels of various proteins to determine the risk of Down’s Syndrome in a fetus. It is more accurate than the combined test and can be carried out from 10 weeks. However, it is not widely available and there is some debate over its usefulness. Therefore the quadruple test is the best option here. This is a blood test that looks for levels of various proteins to determine the risk of Down’s Syndrome in a fetus. It is accurate 75-90% of the time. Source: Fetal anomaly screening lecture, case 8. fetal anomaly screening lecture case 8.pdfIt is important to note that screening tests are not diagnostic of fetal abnormalities and do not replace the need for diagnostic testing. Women who Screen Positive will be offered diagnostic testing by chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis. In this lecture we also looked at the screening programmes for Down’s Syndrome in place in different countries. In the UK women are offered a dating scan and then a combined test or the new NIPT test (non invasive prenatal testing) at 14-20 weeks. At 36 weeks they are offered a repeat NIPT or the Quadruple test. These programmes vary between countries – for example in the US combined test is used instead of the dating scan. Further information on screening programmes can be found on the NHS website. He mentions that the vertigo comes about randomly, even when he is sitting down and not moving, though gets worse if he tries to walk and move. reference: Labyrinthitis is the correct answer as it is a virus causing inflammation of the inner ear (labyrinth), which causes vertigo, hearing loss and tinnitus. It is commonly due to a URI and symptoms can last 2-3 weeks. BPPV is caused by displacement of the otolith crystals and causes positional vertigo. Meneire's disease causes episodic vertigo, hearing loss and tinnitus but has a gradual onset. Vestibular neuronitis is similar to labyrinthitis however it is thought to be caused by a viral infection of the vestibular nerve rather than the inner ear itself. Vestibular paroxysmia is a type of migraine that causes vertigo, although this is rare.  Information taken from: "Diagnosis of Vertigo" lecture in Case 12 and "Inner Ear Problems" article on patient.co.uk.

BPPV is caused by displacement of the otolith crystals and results in positional vertigo. Meniere's disease results in recurrent vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss. reference: Rheumatic fever is caused by group A streptococci (also known as the "Strep" twin). This can be differentiated from the other streptococci mentioned above by its cell wall structure which contains a protein called M-protein. This is what causes the cross reactivity with anti diphtheria toxin. Haemophilus influenzae type b and staph aureus are both Gram Positive Bacteria but neither cause rheumatic fever. Strep pyogenes is also known as the "Strep" twin. It is a Gram Positive Bacteria and causes things like scarlet fever and tonsillitis. instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: A 65 year old man comes into clinic complaining of lower back and leg pain lasting 3 months. He tells you that the pain is worst on walking - particularly when walking down hills and says that the pain is sometimes accompanied by tingling in both legs. When asked if anything relieves his pain he replies ‘rest and sitting in a chair or crouching.’ You decide to complete a back examination. You notice the patient has good flexion of the lumbar spine but extension is limited. The straight leg raise test is negative.   What is the most likely diagnosis? Option A: Peripheral arterial disease Option B: Spinal stenosis Option C: Prolapsed IV disc Option D: Chronic mechanical back pain Option E: Metastatic spinal cord compression The correct answer is Option B.
reference: Spinal stenosis - When the spinal canal (the area through which the spinal nerve roots pass) narrows, it can cause pressure on the nerves. This can be due to degenerative changes in the spine, thickening of the ligamentum flavum (a ligament in the spine), herniation of intervertebral discs, or tumours.  Symptoms - Typically, symptoms get worse when walking (particularly uphill or downhill) or standing for long periods. Relief is often found when sitting down or leaning forward slightly as this reduces the amount of space the nerve roots are taking up.  Diagnosis - It is usually diagnosed after other conditions have been ruled out. Imaging techniques such as MRI may show degenerative changes in the spine or herniated discs. However, these features are not always present. A diagnosis is often made based on a person's history and a physical examination. Treatment - Pain relief (analgesics) and exercise therapy are the main treatments. Injections of local anaesthetic or steroids may also be used. Surgery is very rarely needed. Source: Case 12 'Normal Nerve and Nerve Injury' lecture and 'Neurosurgical Emergency' lecture.  Note: This was covered in the case 12 lecture although I do not recall it being mentioned in the 'Neurosurgical Emergency' lecture.  If anyone has any questions please feel free to ask! References: McCarthy, G. M., & Shacklock, M. (2014). Mechanical Low Back Pain. In Principles and Practice of Pain Medicine (pp. 87-99). Wiley-Blackwell. De Stefani, C., Bisanti, L., & Ossipov, M. H. (2014). Central Nervous System Tumours: Pathophysiology, Presentation, and Management. In Oxford Handbook of Clinical Sceintific Evidence (pp. 320-320). OUP Oxford.
best_explanation: Spinal stenosis - when the spinal canal (the area through which the spinal cord and nerve roots pass) is narrowed. This can be due to degenerative changes in the spine, disc prolapse, facet joint disease or tumours. Symptoms include: Lower back and leg pain which is worse on walking - particularly when going uphill or downhill. Pain may be accompanied by tingling or numbness. Pain is often relieved by sitting down or leaning forward.  Patients with spinal stenosis may also have a reduced range of spinal movement (in flexion and extension). However, the straight leg raise test is usually normal. MRI is useful in identifying the degree of spinal stenosis and whether it is due to degenerative changes, disc prolapse or tumour.   Peripheral arterial disease - Pain in the leg or hips that's worse when walking uphill and relieved when resting or sitting down. The pain is due to poor blood supply to the muscles. Tingling, numbness and sores or ulcers on the toes, feet or legs may also occur.  Prolapsed IV disc - Pain that is worse in extension and relieved on flexion. Pain may be accompanied by tingling in the legs.  Chronic mechanical back pain - Pain that is often worse on walking and relieved on sitting down or leaning forward. Pain may be accompanied by tingling in the legs.  Metastatic spinal cord compression - Pain, numbness and weakness in the legs that's worse on walking. Pain may be accompanied by tingling in the legs.  References:McCarthy, G. M. (2013). Mechanical Low Back Pain. In Low Back Pain (2nd ed., pp. 23-41). instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: A 70 year old female presents in A&E after experiencing some sensory and motor loss in her lower limbs. You suspect she is suffering from an incomplete spinal cord injury. Which cord syndrome is the most likely diagnosis from the following symptoms:Complete motor paralysis below the level of the lesionLoss of pain and temperature at and below the level of injury Intact 2-point discrimination, proprioception and vibratory senses Option A: Central cord syndome Option B: Anterior cord syndrome Option C: Posterior cord syndrome Option D: Brown-Sèquard syndrome Option E: Paget's disease The correct answer is Option B.
reference:
Motor - complete paralysis (Paget's would show some preservation of motor function) Sensory - loss of pain/temp, 2-point discrimination, proprioception and vibration maintained Below - spinal shock (transient heightening of pain and temp below the lesion) Other - X-rays/MRI to confirm diagnosis and rule out tumour or infection which may be causing the cord syndrome. Note: Complete motor paralysis is a reliable indicator of anterior cord syndrome, whereas loss of pain and temp is most characteristic of this condition. Proprioception and vibration are also more commonly preserved in anterior cord syndrome compared to other forms of SCI. Posterior cord syndrome results in loss of pain and temp as well as 2-point discrimination and proprioception, but not vibration. Brown-Sèquard syndrome will result in ipsilateral loss of motor and proprioceptive function, contralateral loss of pain and temp, and maintenance of 2-point discrimination and vibration. Pagets disease shows some preservation of motor function. A useful mnemonic is - Loss Of Pain And Temp, Motor Paralysis, Proprioception and Vibration are commonly preserved in Anterior Cord Syndrome. Whereas in Posterior Cord Syndrome, loss of Pain and Temp plus 2 point discrimination and proprioception are commonly preserved. In Brown Sequard Syndrome there is Ipsilateral loss of motor and proprioception, contralateral loss of pain and temp and maintenance of 2 point discrimination and Vibration. I hope this helps! Spinal Cord Syndromes Worksheet - http://www.medical-institution.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/03/Spinal-Cord-Syndromes.pdf Further reading - https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5566839/pdf/PCAN-24-351.pdf https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537103/ https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medical-and-dentaldiagnosis/brown-sequard-syndrome https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medical-and-dentaldiagnosis/anterior-cord-syndrome https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medical-and-dentaldiagnosis/posterior-cord-syndrome https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medical-and-dentaltherapeutics/pagets-disease-of-the-spinal-cord https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4185063/pdf/PCAN-27-355.pdf https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4585208/pdf/PCAN-28-369.pdf
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Wq3rJhAXBgI
best_explanation: Anterior cord syndrome is the most likely diagnosis given the patient's symptoms. This is a rare vascular syndrome that occurs when there is an interruption of blood supply to the spinal cord. Characteristic symptoms include:Complete motor paralysis below the level of the lesion Loss of pain and temperature at and below the level of injury Intact 2-point discrimination, proprioception and vibratory senses The other syndromes are:Central cord syndrome - results in corticospinal tract damage and produces cervical and thoracic sparringBrown-Sèquard syndrome - causes ipsilateral loss of motor and proprioception and vibratory senses with contralateral loss of pain and temperaturePosterior cord syndrome - results in damage to the dorsal columns and produces a loss of proprioception and vibratory senses on both sidesPageot's disease - results in damage to the dorsal columns and produces a loss of proprioception and vibratory senses on both sides. It is most commonly caused by a tumour compressing the dorsal columns  REF: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537138/table/A5192787/ (it's a very long table but the syndromes listed above are the most relevant)

input: Given question: A baby is born with a cat-like cry, microcephaly and a congenital heart defect. What is the most likely cause? Option A: A duplication on the long arm of chromosome 21 Option B: Trisomy 18 Option C: A partial deletion on the short arm of chromosome 5 Option D: Trisomy 13 Option E: Robertsonian translocation on chromosome 21 The correct answer is Option C.
reference: The answer is C - this is a description of down syndrome (trisomy 21) There are 3 types of Down Syndrome: Trisomy 21 (90% of cases) - this is where there is an extra copy of chromosome 21, in all of your cells. Translocation (5%) - this is where two sections of chromosome 21 break off and get switched around on the same chromosome. Mosaicism (5%) - this is where only some of the cells have an extra copy of chromosome 21. There is also mosaicism with trisomy 18, which is described in option B. Trisomy 18 is the most common trisomy in the foetus (about 75% of cases), followed by Trisomy 21 and then Trisomy 13. Trisomy 13 is described in option D. Robertsonian translocation on Chromosome 21 is an uncommon type of Down Syndrome, accounting for about 3-4% of cases. It occurs when there is rearrangement within the 21 chromosome, so that one part of the chromosome 21 breaks off and attaches to another part of the same chromosome. This leaves the other parts of the chromosome 21 missing. This type is different from a regular translocation because there isn't a piece of another chromosome involved. I found this information in Dr Alex Murray's lecture on chromosomal abnormalities. If anyone wants more info/clarification, just let me know! References: http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vacterl-association/Pages/Introduction.aspx http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/down-syndrome-and-translocation-treatment-and-management.htm http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/downs-syndrome/Pages/Introduction.aspx http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/edwards-syndrome/Pages/Introduction.aspx http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/pataus-syndrome/pages/introduction-and-overview.aspx http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/cornelia-de-lange-syndrome/Pages/Introduction.aspx http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/mowat-dwyer-syndrome/Pages/Introduction.aspx http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/down-syndrome-and-translocation-diagnosis.htm http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/downs-syndrome/Pages/Diagnosis.aspx http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/edwards-syndrome/Pages/Diagnosis.aspx http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/pataus-syndrome/pages/diagnosis.aspx http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/cornelia-de-lange-syndrome/Pages/Diagnosis.aspx http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/mowat-dwyer-syndrome/Pages/Diagnosis.aspx http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/down-syndrome-and-translocation-screening-for-pregnancy.htm http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/downs-syndrome/Pages/Screening-and-testing.aspx http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/edwards-syndrome/Pages/Screening-and-testing.aspx http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/pataus-syndrome/pages/antenatal-screening.aspx http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/cornelia-de-lange-syndrome/Pages/Screening-and-testing.aspx http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/mowat-dwyer-syndrome/Pages/Screening-and-testing.aspx http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/down-syndrome-and-translocation-risk-of-other-birth-defects-and-associated-abnormalities.htm http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/downs-syndrome/Pages/Health-complications.aspx http://www.nhs.uk/conditions
best_explanation: A - is a description of down syndrome B - is Edwards Syndrome C - is Patau Syndrome (the 3 major trisomies) D - is party of the answer E - is another name for down syndrome (i.e. it is the same as answer A) This was covered in the lecture on chromosomal abnormalities in case 7. The most common partial deletions are the 22q11.2 deletion (also can have duplications) which causes Di George syndrome and is associated with Velocardiofacial syndrome. The 22q11.2 deletion causes the same cardiac problems as in C and many of the same facial features as well as occurring with the same frequency. There are many different duplications (of varying sizes) which can cause the same cardiac problems, but not the same facial features. The most common one is the 16p13.1 duplication. There are many different trisomies (with different chromosomes involved) and each has different facial features and other features which are not the same as the other trisomies. The three major trisomies are the most commonly occurring trisomies. There are many different translocations which can occur, but the one described in E is a type of translocation which can cause down syndrome. I hope this helps! instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: A paediatrician is inspecting a newborn child shortly after delivery and notices that the child has a prominent calcaneus on each foot, and has microcephaly with an exaggerated back portion. Further examination reveal a heart murmur in the neonate. The mother had an uneventful pregnancy, however she refused chromosomal testing during her pregnancy. A blood sample is taken and karyotyping is performed revealing an extra chromosome. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Option A: Apert's Syndrome Option B: Edward's Syndrome Option C: Down's Syndrome Option D: Klinefelter's Syndrome Option E: Patau's Syndrome The correct answer is Option B.
reference: Edwards’ syndrome (trisomy 18) is a rare chromosomal disorder in which there is a translocation or fusion of one pair of autosomes to another pair, resulting in a form of monosomy 18. It is also known as trisomy 18. Most cases are sporadic, but about 5%-10% of cases occur as part of a chromosomal balanced translocation. Features shown in the question are characteristic of Edwards’ syndrome: - Prominent forehead with a distinctive shape and flattened nose.- Small jaw, eyes placed far apart, low-set ears, and protruding tongue. - Short stature; neck, arms, and legs are very thin. - Severe intellectual disability. - Heart defects. - An opening in the roof of the mouth (cleft palate). - Hands with two thumbs and missing fingernails. - Feet point away from the body when standing. - Skin between nose and lips forms a single skin fold. - Large tongue. - Breast development in males. - Excessive sweating. - Very fair skin with blue eyes. - Puberty is delayed. Diagnosis is usually made prenatally or postnatally by chromosomal analysis. Treatment is limited to management of symptoms. Prognosis is poor, as most affected infants die within the first year of life. Only 5-10% survive beyond their first birthday. Source: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/edwards-syndrome/ Apert's Syndrome: presents with similar features as Edwards' syndrome, but the main difference is the individual has hyperteleognathy (face is pushed forward), long fingers with large nails and a high pitched scream. Down's Syndrome: presents with a large tongue, brush feet, low-set ears, small chin, single palmar crease and upward slanting palpebral fissures. Klinefleter's Syndrome: presents with primary hypogonadism, pubertal gynaecomastia, tall stature, and normal intelligence. Patau's Syndrome: presents with severe neural tube defect, structural abnormalities, and characteristic facial features including cyclopia (a single eye in the middle of the forehead) and arthryogryposis (joint contractures). Source: http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/chromosomal-abnormalities-and-congenital-malformations-frequency-and-risk.htm http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/trisomy-18-and-21.htm
best_explanation: Apert's Syndrome: presents with a prominent skull, eyes in the sides, hypotonia, developmental delay, and a large tongue. They also have a calcaneus on each foot.  Edward's Syndrome: presents with microcephaly, exaggerated back portion, seal-like face, low-set ears, and a large tongue. They also have a heart murmur, and a calcaneus on each foot.  Down's Syndrome: presents with microcephaly, seal-like face, low-set ears, small eyes with an up slant, single palmar crease, hypotonia, and a heart murmur. They also have a large tongue and a calcaneus on each foot.  Klinefelter's Syndrome: presents with primary hypogonadism, small testes, gynecomastia, and infertility. They also have a developmental delay and muscle weakness.  Patau's Syndrome: presents with severe microcephaly, seizures, developmental delay, structural abnormalities, and severe brain damage. They also have a large tongue.  The answer is B because Edward's Syndrome presents with the same symptoms as the neonate in the question, and chromosomal testing revealed an extra copy of the 18th chromosome. Apert's Syndrome and Down's Syndrome present with a large tongue, but also have other distinct physical features. Klinefelter's Syndrome and Patau's Syndrome are not related to the symptoms in the neonate.  Source: 'Bloom's syndrome' lecture in Case 7, congenital malformations and teratology. Also 'congenital malformations and teratology' plenary in Case 10, chromosomal abnormalities and gene mapping. (I don't own the copyright for the image, it's from google images)

input: Given question: A patient is diagnosed with osteoporosis following a DEXA scan. Of the following pieces of information about this patient, which is NOT a risk factor for the development of osteoporosis? Option A: The patient is 70 years old. Option B: The patient is taking glucocorticoid drugs. Option C: The patient is male. Option D: The patient is a smoker. Option E: The patient has a low BMI. The correct answer is Option C.

reference: This is a classic description of an ruptured aneurysm of the MCA. Nimodipine must be given as soon as possible after the haemorrhage to prevent vasospasm (the main cause of death in this situation). It is usually given via a intra-arterial route. However if this is not available then it should be given IV. It is a calcium channel blocker which prevents spasms of blood vessels. Rupture of an aneurysm is a subarachnoid haemorrhage is indicated by SAH, Hunt and Hess classification grade I-III. Grade I = mild SAH e.g. small leak Grade II = moderate SAH e.g. large leak that has not yet caused a haematoma Grade III = severe SAH e.g. a large haematoma that has formed due to the SAH. This patient would be classed as having a rupture of an aneurysm as he has experienced a thunderclap headache, stiffness of the neck, vomiting and loss of conciousness/swoon. This is indicative of a subarachnoid haemorrhage, grade III. instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: Case 10 (6/8):Which one of the following is part of the diagnostic criteria for diabetic ketoacidosis? Option A: Hypoglycaemia glucose <2.5 Option B: pH >7.45 Option C: WBC in urine (++) Option D: Ketones present >3.0mmol/l Option E: HCO3- >15 The correct answer is Option D.
reference: ketones >3.0mmol/l, bicarbonate <15mmol/l and pH >7.45  Hyperglycaemia >11mmol/l (glucose)  WBCCreatinine >120mol/l (creatine), Urobilinogen >3.5mmol/l (bilirubin) Urinary ketones >3.0mmol/l, acetone +++ in breath, ethanol/acetaldehyde +++ on breath test.  In DKA insulin production decreases, hepatic gluconeogenesis (breakdown of fats to sugars) increases as does glycolysis (sugar metabolism within cells). Without insulin the liver will produce ketones from fatty acid oxidation. These rise in blood and are excreted in urine. As there is less insulin to regulate blood glucose it rises. The osmolarity of the blood increases causing water to move into the urine. This dilutes the blood so that glucose levels appear lower than they actually are. As more water moves into the urine the specific gravity increases and this precipitates out uric acid, other salts and ketones. These are excreted in the urine along with glucose, creatinine and other compounds leading to the characteristic 'ketonic' smell.  Bilirubin, a breakdown product of haemoglobin, is also excreted in the urine. This causes the yellow colour of bruises and jaundice.  In severe DKA there may be a decrease in consciousness due to cerebral edema, dehydration, electrolyte imbalances and acidosis.  Treatment involves giving fluids through an IV to lower the osmolarity of the blood and raise the pH. Insulin is given to stop the production of ketones and reduce the blood sugar level. Bicarbonate is given to increase the pH and HC3O- to increase the bicarbonate level. Sodium chloride is given to replace electrolytes lost due to dehydration. NICE guidelines suggest that potassium should also be replaced if the serum concentration falls below 3.5mmol/l.  Refer to case 10 lecture ‘Diabetes Mellitus’ by Prof. Alan Sinclair for more information.  Source: 'The Diabetic Emergency - Acute Complications of Diabetes Mellitus' lecture by Prof. Alan Sinclair. Medical Biochemistry plenary, case 10.

instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: Dan presents to the GP with back pain. On examination, he has a loss of vibration sensation and proprioception. His MRC is grade 5 in all areas. Pain and temperature sensation are normal. What is the most likely pathology underlying these symptoms? Option A: A tumour of the laminae of some of his vertebrae Option B: Nerve root compression Option C: Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery Option D: Penetrating spinal injury Option E: Reduced blood supply to the centre of the spinal cord The correct answer is Option A.
reference: A tumour of the laminae of some of his vertebrae - this affects the posterior elements of the vertebrae and therefore the posterior column pathways which provide vibration, proprioception and the MRC. Pain and temp are provided by the dorsal/ posterior columns so are not affected.  B: nerve root compression - this affects the spinothalamic pathways which provide pain and temp via the dorsal columns. Vibration is provided by the dorsal columns so would be affected. Proprioception is provided by the spinothalamic pathway but in a more indirect manner as it is relayed through the dorsal columns so would also be affected.  C: occlusion of the anterior spinal artery - this supplies the anterior portions of the spinal cord. Dan would present with motor weakness and loss of pain and temp sensation.  D: penetrating spinal injury - this would likely result in damage to the posterior and anterior horns as well as the dorsal columns. Would present with loss of motor function, pain and temp sensation and proprioception. E: reduced blood supply to the centre of the spinal cord - this would primarily affect the anterior horn cells as well as the dorsal columns. Would present with loss of motor function, pain and temp sensation and proprioception. For more info on the different cell bodies in the spinal cord and their functions see Dr Alex Murray's case 12 lecture on 'the cellular basis of pain'. This was also covered in Dr Colin McCarthy's lecture on 'neurophysiology and pharmacology of pain'. It is also mentioned in Dr McCarthy's lecture on 'neurosciences of pain' that the dorsal columns are particularly important for proprioception. This is because they have a tonotopic organisation similar to the auditory system; different regions of the spinal cord correspond to different frequencies of vibration. This allows us to precisely locate objects in our hands based on the vibrations we feel.
best_explanation: A tumour of the laminae of some of his vertebrae would cause loss of vibration and proprioception as these are sensations that are transmitted by the dorsal/ posterior column pathways. Pain and temperature sensation are transmitted by the spinothalamic pathways which are situated centrally in the spinal cord and so a spinal tumour would not affect these.  B: Nerve root compression would cause loss of nerve conduction, which would be likely to cause a reduction in motor function as well as pain and temperature sensation loss. This would likely present with muscle wasting.  C: Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery would cause a stroke.  D: Penetrating spinal injury would cause immediate loss of sensation and motor function and would likely be very painful. There may also be some spinal cord ischaemia. E: Reduced blood supply to the centre of the spinal cord would cause loss of sensation and motor function. This could be due to a vascular malformation or tumour or could be due to a stroke.  Source: 'Neurosurgical Emergencies' lecture in Case 12 and 'Spinal Cord Ischaemia' lecture in Case 14.  I hope this helps! Let me know if you have any questions.  Dr Coffey's 'Neurosurgical Emergencies' lecture is available on BrightLearner if you want to listen to it again/ haven't got it on your course.  Also, the 'Spinal Cord Ischaemia' lecture is from Case 14 which you may not have got to yet but it might be helpful to listen to it now.  I found it really helpful to understand the pathophysiology of spinal cord ischaemia.  Good luck for the exam everyone!  Lx

input: Given question: Dr Montgomery is helping Callie deliver her baby in the Labour Ward. Callie is in the second stage of labour and is currently in a lot of pain. Dr Montgomery gives her entonox to help relieve the pain of contractions. She turns to her medical student and asks them what is one of the side effects of chronic entonox use? Option A: Addiction Option B: Dry cough Option C: B9 activation Option D: B12 Inactivation Option E: Ataxia The correct answer is Option D.
reference:
Entonox (also known as nitrous oxide) is a gas that is breathed in through the mouth to help relieve labour pains. It works by increasing the levels of pain-free β-endorphins in your brain. Chronic use can lead to B12 inactivation. This means that people who use entonox regularly may become deficient in vitamin B12. This can cause problems with their nervous system and can lead to damage to their spinal cord and brain. In the short term, entonox can also make people feel nauseated and dizzy. They may also experience a dry cough and feel lightheaded. Side effects of entonox are usually reversed when the person stops using it. People who use entonox regularly are not thought to become addicted to it. However, they may find it difficult to stop using it if they have been using it for a long time. This is because they may be worried about the pain returning once they stop using it. entonox does not directly bind to opioid receptors but instead activates B9, an agonist, which produces the analgesic effects. NICE has approved entonox for use in pregnancy, labour and the immediate postpartum period. Source: http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/laboratory-tests-to-diagnose-vitamin-b12-deficiency.htm http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/gas-and-air/pages/introduction.aspx http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/pain-relief-in-labour-and-childbirth/nitrous-oxide/ http://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/308572#_noHeaderPrefixedContent

Let me know if you need anything else!
best_explanation: Chronic entonox use can lead to B12 inactivation.  This is because entonox has a similar structure to B12 and therefore can outcompete B12 for absorption in the ileum.  This can lead to a macrocytic anaemia where there is a decrease in the amount of RBCs (due to the lack of B12) and an increased MCV.  Ataxia is also a symptom of B12 deficiency.  Another side effect of entonox is that it can inhibit the growth of B12 bacteria in the gut.  entonox is also an agonist at the B9 receptor which can cause a dry cough.  entonox is not an addictive drug.  B12 deficiency is a common problem in the elderly and can be exacerbated by chronic entonox use.  This is a common problem in the UK as a lot of people are on long term entonox for chronic pain.  This is why B12 deficiency is something that needs to be screened for in patients on entonox.  This was covered in the case 11 lecture ‘NUTRITIONAL IMBALANCES’. input: Given question: During fertilisation, fusion of the sperm and egg cell membranes causes an increase in the intracellular Calcium of the oocyte. This causes the Cortical reaction. Which of the following describes the cortical reaction? Option A: The breakdown of the acrosomal cap causing a release of enzymes Option B: Depolarisation of the egg cell membrane preventing membrane fusion with further sperm - Primary block to polyspermy Option C: Granules that lie just below the cell membrane fuse with cell membrane and release enzymes hardening the zona pellucida - Secondary block to polyspermy Option D: Meiosis is resumed and the second meiotic division of the egg is completed, forming the definitive oocyte and the second  polar body which is extruded Option E: Glycoprotein coat of spermatozoa is removed, initiating a change in surface charge and reorganisation of the sperm cell membrane The correct answer is Option C.
reference: CORRECT ANSWER - CThe cortical reaction is the process described in option C. It is a series of events that take place within seconds of fertilisation, to prevent polyspermy (the fusion of multiple sperm with one egg). The hardening of the zona pellucida prevents further sperm-egg membrane fusions. The glycoprotiens on the sperm are stripped off and the sperm undergo a functional change in its cell membrane, allowing it to bind to the oocyte.  A & B are incorrect as they describe the acrosome reaction and the plasmalemma surrounding the egg does not have this function. D describes the end of the first meiotic stage E describes the changes that occur to the sperm cell when it undergoes the "capacitation" process prior to fertilization. This allows the sperm to bind to the oocyte. Source: http://cyberbridge.mcb.harvard.edu/mitosis_6.html#mitosis_6_3   Polyspermy is when multiple sperm fuse with one egg. This occurs naturally in some lower organisms such as amoebae. In humans, however, the cortex reaction ensures that only one sperm fuses with one egg. This is important because if multiple sperm fused with one egg, the resulting embryo would have multiple sets of chromosomes and would not be viable.   Source : http://www.fertilityauthority.com/content/what-is-polyspermy-and-the-cortical-reaction/   "In order to ensure that only one sperm fuses with one egg, the egg has a special structure called the zona pellucida. This is hardens around the time of ovulation to become impermeable to sperm. However, just before fertilisation, the zona softens again to allow penetration by sperm. Once a sperm has penetrated, enzymes from the broken acrosome cause the plasma membrane of the sperm to fuse with the outer mitochondrial membrane of the egg. This results in a stable syncytium with the male and female pronuclei at opposite ends. The female pronucleus then degenerates leaving the male pronucleus to continue the journey through the fallopian tube."  Source : http://embryology.med.unsw.edu.au/embryology/index.php/Mitosis_%28B%29  I hope this helps, let me know if you have any questions or need more information. :)  ******has a PhD in Cell Biology******

input: Given question: Dysfunction in which dopamine pathway is thought to cause the positive symptoms of schizophrenia? Option A: Hyperactivation in the mesolimbic tract Option B: Hypoactivation in the mesolimbic tract Option C: Hyperactivation in the mesocortical tract Option D: Hypoactivation in the mesolcortical tract Option E: Hypoactivation in the nigrostriatal tract The correct answer is Option A.
reference: Positive Sx are thought to be caused by hyperactivation in the mesolimbic tract  Negative Sx are thought to be caused by hypoactivation in the mesocortical tract  Cognitive problems are thought to be caused by hypoactivation in the mesolcortical tract and nigrostriatal tract  This is just a rough guide and there is much debate within the literature about the exact nature of dopamine dysfunction in schizophrenia and how it manifests as specific symptoms. These questions are often testing more general concepts so may not reflect the full complexity of the topic. I have included some further reading at the bottom if anyone is interested in delving deeper into the subject. Further Reading: - "Dopamine dysregulation in schizophrenia: neurobiology and treatments" - M.A. Noga (2015) - "The role of dopamine in the pathophysiology of psychosis" - R.S. Kahn (2014) - "D2 receptors and psychotic disorders: focus on dopamine hypofunction" - F.M. Holsboer (2011) https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3566789/ https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3815750/ https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3727731/ Note: All of these articles are behind paywalls I'm afraid, but they should give you an idea of the kind of information that's out there. If you're really interested in the topic, your university or local library might have access to them.
best_explanation: +ve symptoms are thought to be caused by hyperactivation in the mesolimbic tract  -ve symptoms are thought to be caused by hypoactivation in the mesocortical tract  cognitive problems are thought to be caused by hypoactivation in the mesolcortical tract movement problems are thought to be caused by hyperactivation in the nigrostriatal tract  This is all based on the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia which states that there is a imbalance of dopamine in the brain which causes the symptoms of schizophrenia. The hypothesis suggests that there is hyperfunction in the mesolimbic pathway and hypofunction in the mesocortical pathway. It is just one of the many theories that attempt to explain the pathophysiology of schizophrenia.

reference: Cryptosporidium and giardia are both protozoan causes of IID in returning travellers. Other protozoan causes include: Cyclospora and cryptosporidium (both of which can cause chronic disease) as well as many others. Helminths causes of infectious intestinal disease include: ascariasis, trichuriasis, hookworm disease and enterobiasis. These are more commonly seen in children. Bacterial causes of IID include: salmonella, shigella, campylobacter and E coli O157. Viral causes include: norovirus and rotavirus. This was covered in the case 11 lecture ‘INFECTIONS OF PUBLIC HEALTH CONCERN’. Link to a useful powerpoint here: https://www.cdc.gov/ncezid/dpd/pdf/great-expectations-final.pdf. Note that this powerpoint is from the CDC so is quite American-centric but still very informative. It covers all the main infectious intestinal diseases that have been mentioned in the previous answers along with some other ones. It also gives information on transmission, diagnosis and treatment. It’s worth a look if you’re really interested in this topic!
best_explanation: According to the case 11 lecture Giardia is the most common protozoan cause of IID in returning travellers. It is spread via the faeco-oral route and can be contracted from contaminated water. Symptoms include: Abdominal bloating and pain Nausea and vomiting Diarrhoea (may be pale, offensive and fatty) AnorexiaWeight lossFatigue and weakness Treatment is with metronidazole.  Cryptosporidium is also spread via the faeco-oral route and can be contracted from contaminated water. Symptoms are similar to Giardia however treatment is with Nitazoxanide.  Campylobacter is spread via undercooked food and symptoms include: Abdominal pain and cramping Diarrhoea (may be bloody) Nausea and vomiting FeverTreatment is with antibiotics.  Rotavirus is spread via the faeco-oral route and symptoms include: Abdominal bloating and pain Diarrhoea (may be vomity) Nausea and vomitingFeverTreatment is with antibiotics.  Giardia and cryptosporidium can be asymptomatic, therefore it is important for those returning from high risk areas to be tested for these parasites. Source - Case 11 - Infectious Diarrhoea Lecture. input: Given question: If a person takes 3 grams of salt with little water, what changes, if any will occur to the blood osmolality, ADH levels and GFR in a hydrated individual? Option A: Blood osmolality increasesADH levels remains same GFR remains same Option B: Blood osmolality decreasesADH levels decreasesGFR remains decreases Option C: Blood osmolality decreasesADH levels decreasesGFR remains same Option D: Blood osmolality increasesADH levels increaseGFR increases Option E: Blood osmolality increasesADH levels decreaseGFR increases The correct answer is Option D.
reference: 1) Salt intake increases blood osmolality (increases water retention)2) Increased blood osmolality stimulates anterior pituitary to secrete ADH3) ADH causes collecting ducts to insert aquaporins to increase urine concentration4) Dehydration decreases GFR (as less water is filtered out)5) Dehydration negatively impacts ADH levels (secretion reduced due to negative feedback)6) Reduced ADH means collecting ducts remove less water, which means less urine is produced (reduced urine concentration)7) Less water reabsorption means more water is filtrered by kidneys (increased GFR)8) Therefore, when a person takes 3g salt with little water, blood osmolality will increase, ADH levels will decrease, but since they are dehydrated, GFR will remain high/normal. Reference: Crash Course Physiology - Dr Johnson's Lecture on Renal System in the Kidney (from 20 min mark) and Case 12 plenary on ADH/Vasopressin. I also spoke to Dr Johnson about this topic. He said that this was the correct order of events. best_explanation: If a person takes 3g of salt with little water, blood osmolality will increase, ADH levels will increase and GFR will increase.  This is because the increase in osmolality will trigger the secretion of ADH which in turn triggers the GFR to increase the excretion of water.  In a dehydrated patient, ADH levels do not increase and GFR remains low as there is less water to excrete.  This is because the osmolality of the blood is already high so the kidney can conserve water.  However, in a hydrated patient, the osmolality of the blood remains constant and the kidney works to increase the excretion of water.  This is because the kidney cannot conserve water in the blood as the osmolality is already high.  Therefore, the increase in ADH and the increased GFR will increase the excretion of water in the urine.  As there is more water being excreted, the osmolality of the blood decreases and returns to normal.  This process of increasing GFR to excrete water is called the GFR Crest.  It occurs every 20-25 minutes in a normal hydrated patient.  It occurs in the early part of nephron physiology, occurring before the loop of Henle.  In nephrology, the GFR crest is used to measure the patients GFR and is used to diagnose kidney disease.  In chronic renal failure, the GFR crest occurs more frequently.  This is because the kidney cannot conserve water in the blood so the GFR increases excretion of water more frequently.  In acute renal failure, the GFR crest does not occur at all as the kidney cannot excrete water in the urine.  This is because the osmolality of the blood is too high and the kidney cannot conserve water in the blood.  Therefore, the GFR does not increase excretion of water and the osmolality of the blood remains constant.  This is the reason why acute renal failure is a medical emergency as the osmolality of the blood will eventually increase to the point where the brain is affected and the patient goes into a coma. input: Given question: If fertilisation has taken place, at which point post-ovulation does the placenta begin to take over progesterone production from the corpus luteum? Option A: 6-8 weeks Option B: 8-10 weeks Option C: 10-12 weeks Option D: 12-14 weeks The correct answer is Option B.
reference: 8-10 weeks. The placenta takes over from the corpus luteum in terms of progesterone production. Progesterone secretions from the placenta ensure that the endometrial glands are stimulated to secrete nutrients for the developing foetus. If fertilisation does not occur, levels of progesterone will drop and the corpus luteum will degenerate. This process usually occurs between 10-12 days post-ovulation. Source: 'Before We Are Born' by Moore and Persaud. Placental production of progesterone is highlighted on slide 7 of the 'Lec. 1 - Introduction to the menstrual cycle and conception' powerpoint. http://www.fertilemind.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2013/08/Lec.-1-Conception-and-the-menstrual-cycle.pptx.html Also see case 7, lecture 1 - Anatomy of the Breast and Reproductive System.
best_explanation: The placenta takes over from the corpus luteum in terms of progesterone production at around 8-10 weeks post-ovulation. The corpus luteum is then gradually absorbed by the placenta.  Progesterone production continues under the control of the placental cells until around 12-14 weeks, when the placenta is fully formed and able to support the pregnancy. At this point, the production of progesterone moves back over to the ovary, under the control of the anterior pituitary. The ovary continues to produce progesterone throughout the first trimester and beyond, under the control of the hCG. The high levels of progesterone are responsible for many of the physical and biochemical changes that occur during the first trimester, including nausea and vomiting, fatigue, anorexia and constipation. Source: 'Before We Are Born' 6th Edition by Moore and Persaud. Pg. 193.

They are also found in those who have been vaccinated against Hep B.  (Case 11, Microbiology of the GI tract lecture)  For information, glandular fever is caused by Epstein Barr virus, not by Dane particles.  Practising IV drug abuse can lead to Hep B infection, but so can having unprotected sex with someone who has Hep B, receiving a contaminated blood transfusion, and from an infected mother at birth. Sickle cell disease is a genetic condition that affects the production of haemoglobin in red blood cells. They do not have sickle shaped red blood cells, and are generally healthy.  (Case 2, Introduction to Haemotology lecture)  Bacon is not a food that is known to carry Hep B. reference: Astrocytes - regulate blood flow, provide support Ependymal cells - line the CSF-filled ventricles and produce CSF Microglia - act as the first and main form of active immune defense in the central nervous system (CNS) against damaging stimuli such as pathogens, including bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites Oligodendrocytes - produce myelin in the CNS (oligodendrocytes are found in the white matter of the CNS) Neurones - transmit signals throughout the CNS and PNS Hydrocephalus is when there is an abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in the ventricular system of the brain. reference: 1) Keratomalacia- dryness, roughness and scaling of the skin around the nose and mouth 2) Follicular hyperkeratosis- abnormal thickening of the stratum corneum in hair bearing areas 3) Both are symptoms of vitamin A deficiency 4) Vitamin B2- riboflavin deficiency produces keratomalacia, angular chelitis (cracking at the corners of the mouth), glossitis (inflammation of the tongue) and follicular hyperkeratosis 5) Vitamin B3- niacin deficiency produces pellegra which shows as the three Ds : dementia, diarrhoea and dermatitis 6) Vitamin C- scurvy 7) Vitamin D- rickets / osteomalacia 8) Vitamin E- none 9) Vitamin K- none 10) Biotin- none 11) Folate- none 12) Vitamin B12- none 13) Calcium- none 14) Iron- none 15) Magnesium- none 16) Phosphorus- none 17) Iodine- none 18) Zinc- none 19) Copper- none 20) Manganese- none 21) Chromium- none 22) Molybdenum- none 23) Selenium- none 24) Vanadium- none 25) Silicon- none 26) Boron- none 27) Arsenic- none 28) Antimony- none 29) Bismuth- none 30) Polonium- none Source: 'Fundamentals of Nutrition' lecture from Case 11, UNiversity of Otago, Wellington campus. best_explanation: The MMR vaccine is given at 1 year and again at 3 years and 4 months (if not already given at 1 year). The first dose 'sets' the child's immune system up so that when they come into contact with the virus they have already developed antibodies to it. The second dose 'finishes' the immune response. As a result of missing out on the MMR vaccine Kylian was more susceptible to the viral infection that caused SSPE. This demonstrates the importance of completing the primary immunisation programme. If a vaccine is missed it should be given as soon as possible. If this is not possible (e.g. because the child is in hospital) arrangements will be made to give the missed vaccine when the child is discharged. Source: Immunisation lecture case 9. Measles can lead to SSPE as demonstrated in this question. Mumps can lead to orchitis (infection of the testes) in males and deafness in both males and females. Rubella can lead to congenital rubella syndrome which can result in a number of abnormalities in the child including cerebral palsy and growth problems. It is important that as many people as possible are immunised to prevent the spread of these diseases. This is especially important for those who are most at risk (e.g. people who are immunosuppressed). She does some research on the internet before her appointment and asks the GP how her father's condition differs to some of the more common causes of colorectal cancer. The GP informs her that her father's condition is due to a mutation that leads to impaired DNA mismatch repair which causes microsatellite instability whereas the more common conditions that lead of colorectal cancer are most likely due to mutations in tumor suppressor genes.  Given the above information, which of the following conditions is Linda's father most likely to have been diagnosed with? Option A: Attenuated Familial Adenomatous Polyposis Option B: Familial Adenomatous Polyposis Option C: Lynch Syndrome Option D: MUTYH-associated Polyposis Option E: Polymerase-associated Polyposis (PAP) The correct answer is Option C.
reference: A: AFAP is caused by a mutation in the APC gene and leads to the development of numerous polyps in the colon. It is an attenuated form of FAP as it does not have the same level of penetrance as FAP meaning not everyone with the mutation will develop polyps/cancer. B: FAP is caused by a mutation in the APC gene and results in the development of multiple polyps in the colon which can develop into cancer. There is a high degree of penetrance with this condition so almost everyone who has the mutation will develop polyps/cancer. C: This is the correct answer. Lynch syndrome is caused by a mutation in one of four genes - MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2. These genes are all involved in the DNA mismatch repair system. When there is a mutation in one of these genes the system doesn't work properly and this results in microsatellite instability. D: MUTYH-associated polyposis is caused by a mutation in the MUTYH gene. It is similar to FAP as it results in the development of numerous polyps in the colon. However, unlike FAP, it is not caused by a mutation in the APC gene and so is not an attenuated form of FAP. E: PAP is caused by a mutation in the POLYMERASE C gene. This results in the development of numerous polyps in the colon. Unlike FAP and MUTYH-associated polyposis, PAP primarily affects males. input: Given question: Monica presents to her GP with a high fever, muscle weakness and a sore mouth, with bleeding gums. On examination she is hypotensive and tachycardic. Upon reviewing Monica's drug history the GP thinks she might be experiencing agranulocytosis. What is the most likely drug he is attributing to the manifestation of this condition? Option A: Sertraline Option B: Atorvostatin Option C: Bisoprolol Option D: Clozapine Option E: Risperidone The correct answer is Option D.
reference:
Case 10 Pharmacology lightbulb A = no, sertraline is an SSRI so it has an adverse effect of GI disturbances and sexual dysfunction B = no, atorvostatin is a statin with adverse effects of myopathy and hepatic dysfunction C = no, bisoprolol is a beta blocker used mostly in the treatment of angina and cardiac failure D = yes, clozapine has agranulocytosis as an adverse effect E = no, risperidone is an atypical antipsychotic with adverse effects of metabolic changes (weight gain, hyperglycaemia) and movement disorders (akathesia, Parkinsonism) For more information go to: http://www.medicinescomplete.com/ or https://www.uptodate.com/contents/drug-induced- Agranulocytosis is defined as "a bone marrow failure leading to fever >38.3C, neutropenia (<500 cells/mm3), and susceptibility to infection" (off label definition). It is caused by drugs such as clozapine, olanzapine, minocycline, ciprofloxacin, lomefloxacin, ofloxacin and sulfasalazine. If the patient was on any of these drugs and presented with these symptoms then the answer would be yes. However, as it is stated that she is experiencing bleeding gums that points towards clozapine which is the only anti psychotic mentioned that causes agranulocytosis. Other signs of agranulocytosis include recurrent infections, prolonged duration of infection and the presence of petechiae and ecchymoses. (Case 10 pharmacology lightbulb) Important Note: This is not an exhaustive list of all possible drug side effects. It is important to consult the patient’s drug profile or seek specialist advice where necessary. All information should be treated as provisional and subject to change with new evidence. As always, please do your own research and cross check with other sources before making a diagnosis.

input: Given question: Mr Jones has been invited to a 'Cheese and wine' night with his friends from case based learning. He has been taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors for 6 years. Why might he encounter issues on such an evening? Option A: Build up of tryptophan causes loss of consciousness Option B: Excess tyrosine causes loss of libido Option C: Excess tyramine leads to build up of catecholamines Option D: Excess tryptophan leads to build up of serotonin Option E: The interaction of alcohol and MAOIs causes loss of libido The correct answer is Option C.
reference: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors prevent the catabolism of tyramine (and other amines). An increase in tyramine levels may cause a hypertensive crisis as tyramine acts as a potent vasospasm. This is part of the reason why cheese and pickled herring were removed from shop shelves in the UK for a while - they are both high in tyramine. Consumption of tyramine whilst taking MAOIs can be dangerous and has killed people. It is also dangerous to take two monoamine oxidase inhibitors at once as there is no mechanism for the drug to be broken down. This is because the liver does not have the enzyme to break it down and so it builds up in your system. As these are all amino acids found in foods, the build up of these substances in the body can lead to hypertensive crisis. This can be avoided by adhering to a strict diet low in tyramine, tryptophan and tyrosine. However, the interaction between alcohol and MAOIs can cause a hypertensive crisis by the same mechanism. This is because alcohol inhibits the metabolism of tyramine and the build up of tyramine can lead to a hypertensive crisis. For this reason, alcohol should be avoided by patients taking MAOIs. input: Given question: Mr and Mrs Jones are currently awaiting news of whether their latest round of IVF has been successful or not. A problem encountered when carrying out IVF is that it is difficult to recreate the process of Capacitation in vitro.  Capacitation involves the removal of the glycoprotein coat and seminal plasma proteins from the spermatozoa's acrosomal region. For what process during fertilisation is capacitation of sperm a requirement for? Option A: Chemotaxis of sperm towards the oocyte Option B: Formation of the male pronucleus in the oocyte cytoplasm Option C: Penetration of sperm through the Corona Radiata layer of the ovum Option D: Penetration of sperm through the Zona Pellucida layer of the ovum Option E: Prevention of polyspermy The correct answer is Option C.
reference: Capacitation allows sperm to evade the woman's immune system, as the glycoprotiens on the outside of the sperm are removed.  It also allows 2 sperm to fuse with one egg, preventing polyspermy (which would otherwise occur as there are many more sperm produced than can fit within the zona pellucida)  This video explains it much better than me! https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Wt42R7_Nx1Q&list=PL-JgSf8IkHVy-W5A26dMw0eRC_pKKhE6&index=3&t=237s  I hope this helps!
