input: Given question: Mr. Mann comes in to see you at your GP practice. He presents with numbness in the thenar eminence of his palm in addition to pain and tingling in his thumb and lateral two and a half fingers. You diagnose him with: Option A: Klumpke Paralysis Option B: Erb-Duchenne Palsy Option C: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Option D: Claw Hand The correct answer is Option C.
reference: As Mr. Mann is presenting with symptoms which are caused by compression of the median nerve, CTS is the most likely diagnosis. However, it could be either CTS or KP depending on whether the cause of the compression is in the proximal or distal part of the arm. EDP is caused by damage to the axillary branch of the radial nerve just distal to the deltoid muscle. It always presents as a "waiter's tip" deformity of the hand (ulnar deviation of the wrist bones). I made an infographic to help remember these conditions: https://i.imgur.com/7xRmfj1.pngHope this helps! Let me know if you have any questions. Join our community of medical students and junior doctors - follow us on Instagram @the.medical.institute and Facebook @themedicalinstitute to stay up to date with all of our content. #KlumpkeParalysis #ErbDuchennePalsy #CarpalTunnelSyndrome #ClawHand #MedicalEducation #BeyondTheBCLearningObjectives:Compare and contrast the clinical features, causes, and treatment options for Klumpke paralysis, Erb-Duchenne palsy, carpal tunnel syndrome, and claw hand.Case 12 plenary 4. Features of each condition:Klumpke Paralysis:Axonal damage to the distal portion of the median nerve. This usually occurs at the elbow due to compression of the nerve by the humerus bone. Presents with loss of motor and sensory function in the thenar eminence (and sometimes proximally in the forearm). Requires immediate surgical intervention to relieve the compression and allow regeneration of the damaged nerve. Most common cause of axonotmesis in children.Erb-Duchenne Palsy:Axonal damage to the axillary branch of the radial nerve just distal to the deltoid muscle. Usually occurs due to shoulder dystocia during delivery, causing the brachial artery to compress the nerve. Presents with a "waiter's tip" deformity of the hand (ulnar deviation of the wrist bones). Management involves serial casting to correct the deformity and improve function.Carpal Tunnel Syndrome:Compression of the median nerve at the wrist. Can be caused by repetitive use injury, rheumatoid arthritis, pregnancy, hypothyroidism, or tumours. Presents with pain, paraesthesia, and weakness in the thenar eminence and thumb. Treatment includes wrist splints, modification of activities, and sometimes steroid injections.Claw Hand:Congenital absence of the thenar eminence. Can also be acquired as a result of trauma, infection, or neurological disease. Management involves serial casting to improve function and prevent contractures. Learning objectives met:Distinguish between the different types of upper limb peripheral nerve injury (axonotmesis, axonopathy, axonal damage, neuropraxia);Recognise the specific clinical features of each condition;Appreciate the aetiologies of each condition;Understand the principles of nerve physiology and how this impacts on the clinical management of these conditions. #NerveInjury #PlasticSurgery #HandSurgery #OccupationalTherapy #Physiotherapy #RehabilitationMedicine #MedicalStudies #HealthEducation #HealthAndWellbeing #PublicHealth #CommunityMedicine #SocialMediaAdvertising #InstagramMarketing #FacebookAds #BrandManagement #ContentCreation #GraphicsDesign #Infographics #Case12 #Plenary4 #BeyondTheBC#MedEd #Anatomy #Wrist #Elbow #Shoulder #NerveInjury #Rehabilitation #HandSurgery #Neuroscience #UpperLimb #PeripheralNerveInjury #FunctionalOutcomes #Disability #Rehabilitation #PlasticSurgery #NerveRegeneration #Neurorehabilitation #Healthcare #PatientCare #UKNationalHealthService #NHS #Health #Wellbeing #Doctor #Patient #HealthProfessional #MedicalEducation #MedicalStudent #JuniorDoctor #LearningOutcome #Case8 #LowerLimb #Nerve
best_explanation: As Mr. Mann is presenting with symptoms which are caused by entrapment of the median nerve, CTS is the correct answer. However, it is worth noting that this is a very specific set of symptoms and it would be unusual for any clinician to diagnose this combination of symptoms as CTS without investigating further. Normally, a combination of clinical examination and appropriate investigations (such as an EMG) are required to diagnose CTS.  A = Klumpke Paralysis is a form of spastic paralysis. It is due to an injury to the anterior horn of the spinal cord. B = Erb-Duchenne Palsy is a form of spinal paralysis. It is due to an injury to the posterior horn of the spinal cord. Damage to the medial cutaneous branch of the radial nerve can cause a loss of thenar eminence (muscles at the base of the thumb). This is a rare injury and is not relevant to Mr. Mann's symptoms. Damage to the ulnar nerve can cause the opposite set of symptoms (absent thenar eminence and abnormal muscle innervation in the hand). This is known as "hand-foot-genital" syndrome. It is caused by a congenital malformation of the medial cord of the brachial plexus. The malformation causes a disruption of the normal innervation of the muscles in the hand. As a result, the thenar eminence is small and the muscles of the hand are weak. This is the only syndrome which specifically causes the symptoms which Mr. Mann is presenting with. However, it is very rare and it is unlikely that any clinician would diagnose this without extensive investigation.  D = Claw hand is a deformation. It is due to a congenital malformation of the metacarpal bones. The metacarpals are the bones in the hand which connect the phalanges (the bones in the fingers) to the carpals (the bones in the wrist). If the metacarpals do not form properly before birth, the child will be born with claw hand. The correct answer should be C = Carpal Tunnel Syndrome  This was covered in the case 12 lecture "ENTRACTMENT SYND

input: Given question: Nia is a 20 year old patient who has a history of anxiety and depression. She visits her GP as part of her routine medication review. She describes to the GP how after not doing as well as she had hoped in a test, she now believes that she will never get the grades she wants and will never go to uni. Based on this, she has decided not to apply for uni. What is the most likely form of thinking stratergy? Option A: Arbitrary interferences Option B: Black and white thinking Option C: Catastrophising Option D: Personalising Option E: Selective Thinking The correct answer is Option C.
reference: Arbitrary interferences: This involves the misinterpretation of external events so that they seem to conform to some negative conclusion. Black and white thinking: This involves the absence of shades of grey, where everything is either all good or all bad. Catastrophising: This involves assuming the worst possible outcome, without considering any counter evidence or alternatives. Personalisation: This involves taking full responsibility for anything negative that occurs, regardless of whether you are responsible or not. Selective thinking: This involves only focusing on one aspect of a situation and ignoring all others. In this example, Nia is catastrophising by assuming that because she didn't do as well as she wanted, she will never do well enough to go to uni. She is also personalising the situation by assuming it is all her fault and that she has failed. She is also selectively thinking as she is only focusing on the fact that she did not do well in one test, and not considering other factors such as her overall academic record, extra curricular activities etc. which may improve her chances of getting into uni. This is an example of a cognitive distortion. These are errors in thinking that can lead to negative emotions such as anxiety, low mood and anger. They are common in people with mental health issues such as anxiety and depression. There are many different types of cognitive distortions, including arbitrary interferences, black and white thinking, catastrophising, personalising and selective thinking. Identifying these patterns of thinking can help you to challenge and change your negative thought processes. https://www.mind.org.uk/information-support/types-of-mental-health-problems/cognitive-behavioural-therapy-cbt/#.Xa7FxJNKjIU CBT is based on the idea that thoughts, feelings and behaviours are interconnected. It focuses on identifying and changing negative patterns of thinking (cognitive distortions). This is done through a number of techniques, including: - Keeping a diary of thoughts, feelings and behaviours.- Identifying cognitive distortions.- Challenging negative thoughts.- Replacing negative thoughts with more positive and realistic ones.- Developing new ways of thinking and reacting to situations. - Practising relaxation techniques.- Keeping active.- Seeking social support. All information has been taken from https://www.mind.org.uk/information-support/types-of-mental-health-problems/cognitive-behavioural-therapy-cbt/#.Xa7FxJNKjIU . I hope this helps! Let me know if you have any questions or if there is anything else I can help with.

Arbitrary interference is when you change the subject or topic so much that it becomes completely unrecognisable. Black and white thinking is when you see things as completely good or completely bad, without any shades of grey. Personalisation is when you take full responsibility for everything, even things that are outside of your control. Selective thinking is when you only focus on one or two aspects of a situation, whilst ignoring other important aspects.  For this question, the correct answer is C, as Nia is assuming the worst possible outcome will happen, without considering any other possibilities. The inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery is a branch of the SMA. The right and left colic arteries are branches of the inferior mesenteric artery. input: Given question: Professor McGonagall visits the GP. Professor Flitwick and her are expecting a baby. The GP, Professor Snape, would like to give her the flu vaccine since winter is fast approaching and as we know it always snows at Hogwarts. What type of Vaccine would you give her and how would you administer it? Option A: Inactive Virus, Nasal Vaccine Option B: Inactive Virus, Intramuscular Vaccine Option C: Active Virus, Nasal Vaccine Option D: Active Virus, Intramuscular Vaccine Option E: Don't give her a vaccine, because she's pregnant The correct answer is Option B.
reference: The correct answer is B :) Yay! We don't give live/intramuscular vaccines to pregnant women because it could harm the fetus. Pregnant women should only receive inactive/nasal vaccines. This is because the immune system is busy responding to the initial insult of the virus that has been introduced via the nasal route so it doesn't have capacity to react to the vaccine. Therefore the antibodies that are produced are maternal antibodies which aren't as good as ones produced after birth because they haven't had the opportunity to undergo class switching etc. However, maternal antibodies are still better than nothing and can still provide some protection to the baby until their own immune system kicks in. Also, the mothers immunity will be passed on to the child via the placenta for the first few months of life which will help protect the child during the most vulnerable period. This is why it is important to give whooping cough (pertussis), diphtheria and tetanus vaccine when a woman is pregnant to help protect the child before they are born. It is also important to note that any unvaccinated family members or friends should avoid being around the newborn until they have received their vaccinations (first whooping cough vaccination at 2 months). This is because if someone who has not been vaccinated comes into contact with the baby they could potentially catch the illness and pass it onto the baby which could be very dangerous for the child. http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/immunisation-of-pregnant-women.htm http://www.nhs.uk/Conditions/vaccinations/Pages/who-shouldnt-have-the-flu-vaccine.aspx http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vaccinations/pages/vaccinations-and-pregnancy.aspx#close http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vaccinations/pages/whooping-cough-vaccine-and-pregnancy.aspx#close http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vaccinations/pages/diptheria-tetanus-vaccine-and-pregnancy.aspx#close http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vaccinations/pages/giving-vaccines-to-babies.aspx#close http://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/rr5104a1.htm http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17624018
best_explanation: As she is pregnant you can't give her the live, nasal vaccine.  You have to give her the inactive virus, intramuscular vaccine. Why?  Pregnant women are more susceptible to the complications of the flu, so it's important to vaccinate them.  Also, the flu virus is an Influenza B virus.  Influenza B is a intracellular virus, it needs endosomes to grow.  Cells that have endosomes = Cells that the virus can grow in = Cells that are susceptible to the virus = Pregnant women  To grow the virus you need endosomes = To get endosomes you need to be a cell that can form them = Cells susceptible to the virus = Pregnant women  Therefore, pregnant women should be vaccinated with an inactive virus vaccine given as an IM injection.   Source: Vaccine lecture, Case 9, Dr Lisa Wallace.  I tried to find a more specific source but unfortunately couldn't find one. If anyone has any concerns about this please let me know. I'm happy to provide more information.  Note: I did consider using a picture of a wizard for this question but thought it might be too cheesy.  Instead I used a picture of a pregnant woman.  I'm sorry if this offends anyone.  If you have any concerns please let me know.  I'll try to be more mindful in the future.  Thank you.  -Louise

instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: Rupture of which vessels are likely to lead to a subdural haemorrhage? Option A: Superior cerebral veins Option B: Superior sagittal sinus Option C: Meningeal arteries Option D: Vertebral arteries Option E: Cerebellar arteries The correct answer is Option A.
reference: 1. rupture of superior cerebral veins can lead to a subdural haemorrhage 2. rupture of the superior sagittal sinus can lead to a traumatic brain injury 3. meningeal arteries supply the meninges 4. rupture of the vertebral arteries can result in an aneurysm 5. rupture of the cerebellar arteries can result in an epidural hematoma subdural haemorrhages are commonly seen in the setting of alcohol excess (sometimes the patient doesn't even know they have bled), and can often be treated by removing the source of bleeding and allowing the haemostasis system to work. epidural haemorrhages tend to occur in younger patients and are more commonly due to rupture of an artery (often a branch of the internal carotid) - these haemorrhages usually aren't associated with a clear history of trauma. traumatic brain injuries are associated with skull fractures or direct impact to the head - they are not the same as a subdural haemorrhage. an aneurysm is when part of the blood vessel wall breaks, causing a localized bulge. this can result from rupture of one of the vertebral or internal carotid arteries. an epidural hematoma is a collection of clotted blood that forms between the dura mater and arachnoid mater of the meninges, most commonly occurs due to a ruptured cerebral artery (one of the branches of the internal carotid). there is often a lucid interval where the patient seems fine for several hours after the incident. during this time the clot swells and puts pressure on the surrounding brain tissue, leading to secondary brain damage. consequently the patient will often succumb to this 2-3 weeks post injury. if however the patient survives longer than 3 weeks they have a good chance of making a full recovery. in summary: subdural = common in alcoholics, treated by removing source of bleeding and allow haemostasis system to work epidural = young pts, due to rupture of an artery (branch of IC), no clear history of trauma traumatic brain injury = s/p direct impact or skull fracture an aneurysm is a bulge from the blood vessel wall caused by wall breakage rupture of a cerebral artery may cause an epidural hematoma = clotted blood between the meninges, often due to rupture of the internal carotid artery. there is often a lucid interval where the patient seems fine for several hours after the incident. during this time the clot swells and puts pressure on the surrounding brain tissue, leading to secondary brain damage. consequently the patient will often succumb to this 2-3 weeks post injury. if however the patient survives longer than 3 weeks they have a good chance of making a full recovery.
best_explanation:
Rupture of the superior cerebral veins is most likely to lead to a subdural haemorrhage. This is because these veins have relatively thin walls and are close to the surfaced of the brain. Rupture of the superior sagittal sinus is most likely to lead to a herniation of the brain (coup injury).  The meningeal arteries are relatively small and are unlikely to cause significant haemorrhage following rupture.  Rupture of the vertebral arteries would most likely lead to an epidural haemorrhage.  Rupture of the cerebellar arteries is unlikely to result in a haemorrhage due to the location of these vessels.  This information is from the neuroanatomy practical in case 12. input: Given question: Select the approximate heterozygous frequency for an autosomal recessive disorder with a frequency of 1 in 2500 live births Option A: 1/25 Option B: 1/50 Option C: 1/75 Option D: 1/100 Option E: 1/125 The correct answer is Option A.
reference:
1/25 because AR = dominant / (dominant + recessive) and if you have 1 dominant and 1 recessive the ratio is 1/1 which equals 1 If you have 1 dominant and 1 recessive you have 2 alleles and the formula would be 2/2 which equals 1 Therefore you have an autosomal recessive disorder with a carrier frequency of 1/25 or 4% This is a general approach, not just for autosomes but for any chromosome The above link also explains it very well using examples https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YE8f6OzK9eA&t=2s I would also recommend reading Dr Alex Murray's lecture on Family History and Probabilities as this will help you understand this concept further Link to his lecture http://www.hps.cam.ac.uk/library/courses/genetics-and-probabilities/family-history-and-probabilities/family-histories-probabilities-lecture-part-a#_ftn17 'The Hardy Weinberg Equilibrium' lecture from case 7 also helps explain this concept further https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIpuiX8Xmwk&t=2s
This video explains how to calculate the carrier frequency of an autosomal recessive disorder.  The method of calculating the carrier frequency is using the Hardy Weinberg equation, where p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1, where p is the frequency of the general population and q is the frequency of the disease.  In an autosomal recessive disorder, p = 1 and q = 1/2500, therefore the carrier frequency is 1/25.   This was covered in the Family History and Probabilities lecture, although it wasn't explained in as much detail as this video.  It is important to note that this method is only for autosomal recessive disorders, and for other types of genetic disorders, different methods need to be used.  The video also shows how to work out the risk of being a carrier, which is 2/3.  This was also covered in the Family History and Probabilities lecture.   Overall, this video provides a good summary of how to calculate the carrier frequency of an autosomal recessive disorder, and is useful for revisiting the content of the Family History and Probabilities lecture.   However, it is quite long and some parts are a bit slow, so it may be more beneficial to skip forward to the relevant bits.   Additionally, there are some slight inaccuracies in the way the information is presented, such as when it says "if you have 1 dominant and 1 recessive the ratio is 1/1 which equals 1", it should say 1/2 which equals 1 instead.   However, overall this is a helpful resource.   It is recommended to watch the 'Hardy Weinberg Equilibrium' lecture from Case 7, as this goes into more depth about the Hardy Weinberg equation and its applications.   Link to the 'Hardy Weinberg Equilibrium' lecture from Case 7https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIpuiX8Xmwk&t=2s   Link to the Family History and Probabilities lecture https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YE8f6OzK9eA&t=2s   Link to the Genetics and Probabilities folder on LSE VLE https://www.lshtmcdonald.ac.uk/course-material/genetics-and-probabilities/   Link to the Family History and Probabilities Workbook https://www.lshtmcdonald.ac.uk/course-material/genetics-and-probabilities/workbooks/family-history-and-probabilities/   Link to the Case 7 folder on LSE VLEhttps://www.lshtmcdonald.ac.uk/course-material/case-7/   Genetics tutorial on LSE VLE pagehttps://www.lshtmcdonald.ac.uk/study-support/resources/genetics-tutorial?itemID=1000038112231&moduleId=1000037947812&contentId=1000038112231&parentFolderId=1000037947812&
best_explanation: The Hardy Weinberg equation must be upheld: p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1p = frequency of dominant alleleq = frequency of recessive allele  Therefore: p + q = 1p2 = frequency of dominant allele (1/2500)2 = 1/62500q = 1 - 1/62500 = 1/32500 Therefore p = 1/3 and q = 2/3 Heterozygous frequency = p2 = (1/3)2 = 1/9  Therefore the answer is 1/9 or 1/2500 as the autosomal recessive disorder has a frequency of 1 in 2500 live births.  If it helps, think of it as the autosomal recessive disorder has a frequency of 1 in 2500 live births, so the frequency of the dominant allele is 1/2500 and the carrier frequency is 1/2500. The Hardy Weinberg equation must be upheld, so 1/2500 = p and 1/2500 = 2pq. Therefore p = 1/2500 and q = 2/2500 = 1/12500. Finally, p2 = (1/2500)2 = 1/62500 and q2 = (2/2500)2 = 1/12500. Therefore p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1/25002 + 2(1/2500)(2/12500) + (1/12500)2 = 1/62500 + 2/12500 + 1/12500 = 1/2500. So p + q = 1/2500 = 1/2500 as it must be.  Frequency x probability = probability x frequency.  Therefore the answer is 1/2500.  I hope this makes sense.  Let me know if you have any questions.  I will try to help

instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: Stimulation of beta adrenergic receptors via noradrenaline on ventricular myocytes causes a number of physiological changes. These include increased Ca2+ movement into the cell (Via L-type Ca2+ channels), causing increased Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Which receptor on the SR is stimulated to cause this CICR (Calcium induced calcium release)?What effect will this have on the cardiac cycle? Option A: HCN4 channels Increased Chronotropy Option B: Ryanodine receptorsIncreased Inotropy and accelerated Lucitropy Option C: HCN4 channels Increased Inotropy Option D: Ryanodine receptors Decreased Inotropy and accelerated Lucitropy Option E: HCN4 receptors Increased Lucitropy The correct answer is Option B.
reference: Increased beta adrenergic signaling (Noradrenaline) stimulates the ryanodine receptors on the sarcoplasmic reticulum. This causes increased Ca2+ release from the SR which increases the rate of contraction of the heart. This occurs as CICR (Calcium Induced Calcium Release) occurs when the levels of calcium in the cytosol are high enough to bind to the Ryanodine receptor on the SR. This results in increased inotropy (contractility) and accelerated lucitropy (relaxation). A - HCN4 channels are voltage gated Na+ channels that are activated at more depolarized potentials (around +50mV) B - Correct! Activation of beta adrenergic receptors leads to increased cyclic AMP production which activates Protein kinase A. PKA then phosphorylates the phosphorylation domain on the Ryanodine receptor on the sarcoplasmic reticulum. This causes the effects stated above C - HCN4 channels increase the "speed" at which depolarizations occur (chronotropy)D - Decreasing inotropy would result in a weaker contractile force of the heart. Accelerating lucitropy would mean that relaxation occurs faster, potentially before the next contraction has occurred. Both of these would be undesirable effectsE - HCN4 channels are also known as the funny current because they are slow to activate but once activated, the current remains active for a longer period of time. This results in depolarizations occurring relatively quickly (increased chronotropy) However they do not help with contraction as they are carried out onto the cell during an action potential. Also they are carried by T-type calcium channels which are voltage gated. As the ventricular myocytes have a very small capacitance (resulting in a fast time constant) it means that it takes a long time for the T-channels to deactivate and therefore a steady state is never reached. This means that even though depolarizations may occur quickly, the amplitude of the action potential is reduced and therefore cannot be used to trigger a contraction. Source: Regulation of excitation and contraction in the heart lecture from Case 13. Also contains information about the slow inward current (SIC) which is carried by T-type calcium channels and is involved in pacemaking in the AV node. Additionally, the delayed rectifier potassium currents (IKr) are responsible for the rapid repolarization phase of the action potential in the ventricles. http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2661778/table/T1/contains/tbl1/ This website explains the role of different ion channels in the heart and their functions in detail. It also includes a section on the effects of various drugs on these ion channels.
best_explanation: HCN4 channels - Increased Chronotropy. These channels are Na+ channels that allow Na+ to flood into the cell during the action potential. This increases the slope of the pacemaker potential and increases the frequency of action potentials. Ryanodine receptors - Increased Inotropy and accelerated Lucitropy. These receptors are found on the SR and are stimulated by noradrenaline via beta adrenergic receptors. They release more Ca2+ from the SR which increases the amplitude of the action potential and increases the contractility of the myocyte.  CICR is calcium induced calcium release from the SR. A) HCN4 channels - this would increase chronotropy, not inotropyB) Ryanodine receptors - correct as this increases inotropy and lucitropyC) HCN4 channels - these increase the slope of the pacemaker potential and increase the frequency of action potentials, not inotropyD) Ryanodine receptors - the opposite effect as this would decrease inotropy and accelerate lucitropyE) HCN4 receptors - these increase the slope of the pacemaker potential and increase the frequency of action potentials, not inotropy. Lucitropy is the rhythmic beating of the heart and is determined by the AV node and the refractory properties of the myocytes. Increasing the slope of the pacemaker potential will not directly increase lucitropy.  Source: Regulation of the Cardiac Cycle Lecture, Case 12. Also, Noradrenaline and Adrenoceptor Agonists slide from Case 12. (Beta Blockers and Calcium Channel Blockers also decrease inotropy)  The effect of adrenaline is to increase the force of contraction and the heart rate. This is achieved by increasing calcium entry into myocytes via L-type calcium channels and by increasing the amount of calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum via ryanodine receptors.  Source: Dr Yousef's Lecture; 'PHYSIOLOGY OF THE CARDIAC CYCLE'  (PPT slide 25)

instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: The Pudendal nerve is often blocked during foreceps delivery to provide pain relief. What are the spinal nerve roots of the Pudendal nerve? Option A: L2, L3 and L4 Option B: L4, L5 and S1 Option C: S1, S2 and S3 Option D: S2, S3 and S4 Option E: S3, S4 and S5 The correct answer is Option D.
reference: 答えはDの「s2, s3 and s4」です。refrence: http://teachmeanatomy.info/lower-limb/nerves/pudendal-nerve/ Note: There are 2 pudendal nerves, a superior and inferior pudendal nerve. The superior pudendal nerve is S2, S3 and S4 and the inferior pudendal nerve is L2, L3 and L4. However, it is the inferior pudendal nerve that is usually blocked during forceps delivery. Another note: The pudendal nerve provides motor to the skeletal muscles in the perineum, urethra, external anal sphincter, external urethral sphincter and part of the levator ani. It also has sensory supply to the genitalia, perineum, urethra and rectum. Coffey lecture, case 8.
best_explanation: The pudendal nerve (S2, S3 and S4) can be blocked with lidocaine to reduce pain during forceps delivery. The pudendal nerve roots are at S2, S3 and S4. The pudendal nerve provides sensation to the genitalia, perineum and anal skin. It also provides muscular branches to the external urethral sphincter and the external anal sphincter. The anal sphincters are often sutured shut after delivery to bring the baby's head in contact with the pelvic floor to help progress labour. This is called a 'sphincter's catch' and is a sign that the baby's head is in the pelvis and labour is likely to progress quickly. The pudendal nerve is also at risk of injury during a spinal analgesia, as the anaesthetist may inadvertently inject the analgesia into the nerve rather than around it. This can result in paralysis of the external urethral sphincter and anal sphincter.  Information taken from 'Anatomy Practical' by Andrew Moore and 'Anaesthesia and Analgesia in Childbirth' by Declercq and Joris.

input: Given question: The carnitine shuttle is responsible for transferring Acyl-CoA molecules through the mitochondrial membrane to be used in beta-oxidation. The TAG synthesis is the synthesis of TAG from FFA and glycolytic intermediates in the cytosol. Beta-oxidation is the process of breaking down an Acyl-CoA molecule, which is derived from FFA, into acetyl-CoA.  This process produces 2 molecules of CO2 and 1 molecule of NADH.  The acetyl-CoA produced in beta-oxidation can then enter the TCA-Cycle in the mitochondria to produce more ATP. input: Given question: The placenta is formed from .... Option A: The embryo’s mesenchymal cells Option B: The mother’s endometrium only Option C: The mother’s endometrium and the embryo’s chorionic membrane Option D: The mother’s myometrium and the embryo’s umbilical cord Option E: The conceptus and the mother's myometrium The correct answer is Option C.

best_explanation: The correct answer is C. The placenta is formed from the mother's endometrium and the embryo's chorionic membrane. The embryonic part of the placenta is called the chorion, and the maternal part is called the decidua. The placenta provides a barrier between the maternal circulation and the foetal circulation, allowing for the exchange of oxygen and nutrients without allowing for the mixing of the two bloodstreams. The placenta also provides a route for the transfer of foetal waste products and excess heat from the foetus to the maternal bloodstream, as well as serving as a site for the production of steroids and other substances crucial to the foetus's development. input: Given question: To which of the following does RNA polymerase copy genetic information from? Option A: Leading strand Option B: Protein strand Option C: Coding Strand Option D: Non-coding strand Option E: TATA box The correct answer is Option D.
reference: RNA polymerase reads genetic information from the non-coding strand because this is where the promoter is found.  The other answers are all incorrect because they represent different parts of the DNA double helix: leading and protein strands = chromosome strand (not part of the helix) coding and non-coding strands = complementary strands of the helix TATA box = found upstream of gene, on the same strand as the gene. Transcription starts at a site just downstream of the TATA box. Knowing that RNA polymerase reads the non-coding strand means that transcription proceeds in the opposite direction to replication. This is called counter-clockwise. Replication proceeds in the other direction - clockwise. This is important for DNA repair. Sources: Gilbert's "The World of Genetics" and "Essential Clinical Anatomy" by Richard S. Irving and Stephen M. Morrissey. --136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.41 06:45, 8 April 2007 (UTC) 136.150.82.
best_explanation: RNA polymerase reads genetic information from the non-coding strand.  The leading strand is the synthetic strand which is synthesised continuously in the same direction as the cell's replication.  The protein strand is the strand which is synthesised continuously in the opposite direction to the cell's replication.  The TATA box is a DNA structure which acts as a binding site for RNA polymerase.  Coding strand is also known as the template strand.  This strand contains the genetic information which is read by ribosomes to synthesise proteins.  The non-coding strand is the complementary strand of DNA which does not contain the genetic information for proteins.  Source: Gilbert's Evolution of Life lecture in case 11.  Also the DNA and RNA structure and function plenary in case 11.  Additionally the DNA and Protein Structure and Gene Function plenary in case 12. input: Given question: Velma the Virus has a plan. Using her cunning, skills and womanly good looks, she intends to infiltrate the defences of the hairy medical student she has just entered, and then cause havoc and woe. But first, she must evade the student's sentinel cells, lest they present her antigens to their commanders. Wait! What's that?  Which of these is NOT a sentinel cell? Option A: Macrophage Option B: Microglial cell Option C: Natural killer cell Option D: Dendritic cell Option E: Langerhans cell The correct answer is Option C.
reference: Sentinel cells are: -Macrophages -Microglial cells -Natural killer cells -Dendritic cells -Langerhans cells  Velma will have to be careful not to get spotted by any of these, especially if she tries to leave a calling card...  Case 12: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity (Part II)   Dr Coffey's lecture: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Wt42R5J3jXs&feature=plcp  Innate immunity: -Barriers (skin, mucous membranes, acidic environment, bile salts, radiation)-Physical (like macrophages and neutrophils)-Chemical (enzymes, free radicals)-Immunological (antimicrobial peptides, complement system, lectins, receptors)-Microbiota (lactobacillus, bifidobacterium, enterococci) Adaptive immunity: -Specificity (antigen-specific, remember the last 5 bugs that tried to off you?) -Memory (longer response because of pre-existing immunity, affinity greater) -Cell mediated (CTL, CD8+, CD4+) -Humoral (antibodies, B cells, IgG)  Dr Coffey also mentioned a type of T cell called a Tfh cell which is involved in B cell responses.  This was covered in the second part of his lecture but I haven't been able to find it on YouTube. If anyone knows where I can find it please let me know!  Case 13: Coffey Lecture- Functions of the Immune System   Dr Coffey's lecture: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Wt42R5J3jXs&feature=plcp   The immune system has two main functions: -Elimination (removal) of a pathogen -Protection of the host from subsequent reinfection by the same pathogen  Dr Coffey also mentions a third, which is protection of the host from unrelated diseases.  This is called 'immunosuppression' and occurs when there is a decrease in the overall immune response. This can occur naturally in some circumstances, such as during pregnancy, but can also occur as a result of disease.  For example, HIV infection causes immunosuppression, as does cancer.  Case 14: T & B Lymphocytes    T and B lymphocytes are types of white blood cells that play a vital role in the immune response. T lymphocytes recognize and target specific proteins (or pieces of them) from viruses or other infectious agents, while B lymphocytes produce antibodies that specifically recognize and bind to those same proteins. Antibodies are proteins produced by B cells that recognize specific pathogens or toxins. When an antibody binds to a pathogen, it can prevent it from spreading or causing harm. Antibodies can also help to neutralize or remove bacterial or viral toxins.  T and B cells can work together to destroy virus-infected cells. T cells can recognize infected cells and kill them, while B cells can produce antibodies that can mark the virus or infected cell for destruction by other parts of the immune system. Hope to see you there! NK cells are activated by IL-12, secreted by macrophages and dendritic cells. NK cells are able to kill virally infected cells immediately by the release of perforins and granzyns, forming a pore in the target cell's membrane. instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: Which Sunderland classification of nerve injury is described by the following?  - loss of axonal and endoneurial continuity- perineurium intact - no conduction Option A: I Option B: II Option C: III Option D: IV Option E: V The correct answer is Option C.
reference: - loss of myelin sheath (axonotmesis) - no conduction  - loss of axonal and endoneurial continuity- perineurium and epineurium intact - some conduction  - complete transection of nerve- no continuity or conduction  - nerve partially severed with a large gap - no conduction Axonotmesis is the most common type of nerve injury seen in clinical practice. It often results from trauma to the nerve at or near the site of injury. In these cases, there may be associated soft tissue injury, including damage to the endoneurium and perineurium. Epineurium remains in tact to allow for possible regeneration. Axonotmesis often heals spontaneously without intervention; however, surgical repair may be necessary in certain cases. Neurotmesis is a more severe nerve injury and results from complete transection of the nerve. There is no continuity or conduction in this type of injury. In some cases, the neurotmesis may be surgically repaired, but frequently the nerve must be trunked, a procedure in which a section of the nerve is removed and replaced with a nerve graft. This procedure is performed less commonly than it was in the past, due to the development of better methods of repairing the nerve. In general, the prognosis for nerve recovery is good following axonotmesis, while the prognosis following neurotmesis is poor. Sunderland Classification of Nerve Injury: I = Axonotmesis II = Partial nerve severance with a large gap III = Loss of axonal and endoneurial continuity with perineurium and epineurium in tact IV = Complete nerve severance V = mixed pattern of injury taken from Case 12 Plenary 1: Nerve Injuries lecture. Pg. 38-47. For more information: http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10691565 'Nerve injury' lecture from Case 12 Plenary 1. Pg. 38-47.
best_explanation: I = myelin sheath damage II = axon and endoneurial damage, perineurium intact III = axon, endoneurium and perineurium damage, no conduction IV = axon, endoneurium, perineurium and epineurium damageV = complete nerve transection and neurotmesis Epineurium is the outermost layer of the nerve, and is usually damaged in nerve injuries IV and V.  Sunderland classification is the most commonly used system for describing nerve injury.  Axonotmesis is the most common nerve injury and is classified as Sunderland I. Neurotmesis is classified as Sunderland V.  Axonotmesis is a nerve injury to the nerve axon, endoneurium and perineurium.  Neurotmesis is a nerve injury where the nerve is completely transected.  Axonotmesis can lead to neurotmesis if the nerve is not repaired within 60 minutes of the injury.  From the nerve injury lecture in case 12. instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: Which antibody type is particularly important in preventing adhesion of viruses to the apical membrane of enterocytes? Option A: IgA Option B: IgD Option C: IgE Option D: IgG Option E: IgM The correct answer is Option A.
reference: IgA is found in body secretions. It is particularly important in preventing adhesion of viruses to the apical membrane of enterocytes. Viral attachment can lead to colonization and eventual rotavirus-induced diarrhea. Viral attachment can also lead to respiratory tract infections.  IgD is found on the surface of naive B cells. It functions in the activation of B cells through its interaction with the CD21/31 complex.  IgE is involved in antigen recognition and mediator release from mast cells. Mast cell degranulation leads to bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, and increased mucus production in asthmatics.  IgG is the antibody of choice for neutralizing virus and bacteria in extracellular fluid. It is also the only antibody type that can cross the placenta (Lec. "Blood groups in Man") IgM is the first responder in infections. It activates complement pathway and has a pentameric structure. Source: Dr. H. L. Duhamel's Immunology Phase 3 lecture. Also "Hence, IgA is particularly important in preventing adhesion of viruses to the apical membrane of enterocytes" - Dr. R. S. Glassman's Case 8 lecture on "Intestinal Transport" (both lectures are available on Case 8)
best_explanation: IgA is particularly important in preventing adhesion of viruses to the apical membrane of enterocytes. The other antibodies all have different functions and are produced in different parts of the body.  IgG is produced in the bone marrow and is the only antibody type which can cross the placenta. It is also the only antibody type which can be produced in response to a vaccine.  IgA is produced in body secretions.  IgM is produced in the bone marrow and is the first responder to a suspected infection. It causes inflammation at the site of the infection and attracts macrophages and neutrophils.  IgD and IgE are both produced in the bone marrow. IgD is the only antibody type which is expressed on the B cell surface. It is thought to act as an adhesion molecule, allowing B cells to interact with other cells. IgE is involved in allergy and parasite immunity. It is also the only antibody type which can be produced in response to a food allergen.  I put this in the trivia category, but it is actually quite important as adhesion of viruses to the apical membrane of enterocytes is a key step in the spread of infection through the intestinal tract. Viruses can then penetrate the enterocytes and gain access to the lymphatic system.  Information from 'Immunological responses to viral infection of the GI tract' lecture in Case 9. input: Given question: Which of the following is likely to cause osmotic diarrhoea? Option A: Cholera infection Option B: Crohn's disease Option C: Coeliac disease Option D: E. coli infection Option E: Giardia The correct answer is Option C.
reference: Cholera = Watery stools with a high volume and electrolyte loss, often acquired from contaminated water. Can lead to severe dehydration/shock. Treatment is oral rehydration therapy. Crohn's/Coeliac = Diarrhoea is bloody and associated with abdominal cramps and fever. Patients may have arthralgia and weight loss. E. Coli = Mucous and possibly blood-stained diarrhoea, abdominal pain and fever. Treat with antibiotics if severe. Giardia = Normally asymptomatic, but can cause watery diarrhoea, abdominal bloating and anorexia. Treated with metronidazole. Source: Case 11 "Form and Function in the GI Tract" tutorial and Dr Yousef's lecture "Intestinal Microbiota and Diarrhoea" (week 12). Note: I did not include Irritable Bowel Syndrome as this was covered in the case 10 small group discussion. Also, C. Diff infection was not mentioned in the tutorial/lecture so I excluded it.
best_explanation: Coeliac disease causes osmotic diarrhoea as the small intestine is unable to absorb water from the chyme, due to damage to the villi. This is because the villi are flattened and the brush border enzymes are reduced in number. The brush border enzymes break down the large molecules from the chyme into smaller ones, which are then absorbed by the enterocytes. However, since there are fewer enterocytes (due to the damage to the villi), there is less surface area for absorption. The unabsorbed water is then drawn into the lumen of the GI tract by the osmotic effect of the unabsorbed molecules, resulting in diarrhoea. Giardia infection can also cause osmotic diarrhoea as the parasite produces a lot of osmotic material. Vaccines for Cholera and E. coli are available. There is no vaccine for Crohn's or Coeliac disease, but a cure for Cholera is imidazole (antibiotic) and oral rehydration therapy. reference: Aldosterone: -Stimulates the Na+/K+ ATPase in the kidney to increase sodium reabsorption-Stimulates the H+/K+ ATPase in the stomach and intestine to increase hydrogen chloride (gastric juice) and potassium secretion-Increases blood volume and pressure by increasing blood flow through increased blood vessel diameter-Increases plasma [Na+], [K+], [HCO3-], and [Cl-]-Decreases plasma [Argentaffin] Case 10 Plenary 4: Endocrine system lecture- Dr Shore  Aldosterone: -Stimulates the release of ADH (antidiuretic hormone)-Increases water retention by the kidneys-Increases sodium and bicarbonate reabsorption, and potassium secretion by the kidneys-Increases blood volume and pressure by increasing blood flow through increased blood vessel diameter-Increases plasma [Na+], [K+], [HCO3-], and [Cl-]-Decreases plasma [Argentaffin] Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) Lecture- Case 12 Plenary 5: Endocrine system lecture- Dr Shore  Key points: -RAAS is under negative feedback control of angiotensin II (and probably also bradykinin).-The main effect of angiotensin II is to increase blood pressure by vasoconstriction in peripheral blood vessels and the renin-angiotensin loop increases as a result.-Aldosterone has a number of effects which all tend to increase blood volume and therefore blood pressure. This is why aldosterone is sometimes called "the anti-hypertensive hormone".-The main stimulus for aldosterone release is increased Na+ in the systemic circulation, such as occurs with ACE inhibition (e.g. ramipril).-ACE inhibitors are therefore contraindicated in patients with heart failure because they decrease aldosterone, which tends to drop blood pressure, whereas diuretics, which increase aldosterone, are often used to treat heart failure. Source: Crash Course Pharmacology lecture "DRUGS USED TO TREAT HEART FAILURE" case 12 plenary 5. Also case 10 plenary 4 endocrine system lecture.  Dr Shore's lectures on the RAAS and pharmacology of heart failure were very helpful in understanding this topic. It shows the effects of increasing concentrations of AngII on renin, aldosterone, vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone), and atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP). AngII also induces the expression of ACE2 in the liver. Angiotensin III has been studied less than other components of the RAAS system but it appears to have a role in promoting Na+ reabsorption in the collecting duct in the kidney.  http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2978647/#!po=7.3446  The RAAS system acts to conserve salt and water, primarily by increasing blood pressure. This is achieved partly by the actions of aldosterone, which acts on the kidney to increase Na+ and water reabsorption, and on the distal colon to increase K+ absorption. The Kidney also secretes renin, which acts on the liver to produce angiotensinogen, which is then converted by renin to angiotensin I. Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) in the lung converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, which has powerful vasoconstrictor and pressor effects, causing blood vessels to narrow. Angiotensin II also stimulates the production of aldosterone, so that the levels of both rise together. Angiotensin II also stimulates vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) release in the posterior pituitary gland. Vasopressin acts on the kidney to promote water reabsorption and thus prevent dehydration. C - Sodium ions (Na+) are also reabsorbed along with potassium ions (K+).  D - Bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) are reabsorbed in the distal tubule and collecting duct. instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: Which of the following is not absorbed in the duodenum? Option A: Calcium Option B: Iron Option C: Glucose Option D: Bile salts Option E: fructose The correct answer is Option D.
reference: Calcium - absorbed in the intestines by TRPV channels (more calcium is absorbed here than any other nutrient) and in the duodenum by NEUTRAL TRANSPORTERs. Iron - almost all of the iron we eat is absorbed in the duodenum via H+ as ferritin or transferrin. Glucose - 90% of glucose is absorbed in the duodenum. Bile salts - some bile salts are absorbed in the distal ileum but most are just eliminated. Fructose - 75% of fructose is absorbed in the first half of the small intestine (the level of absorption depends on the amount consumed). Polysaccharides are broken down to monosaccharides in the lumen of the SI before they are absorbed. Monosaccharides can diffuse across the enterocytes basolaterally whereas polysaccharides require hydrolysis within the enterocyte. This is why the rate of absorption of a given amount of glucose is faster than that of a polymer like starch. The monosaccharide uptake then undergoes transporters specific for each type of sugar.  Bile salts are absorbed in the distal ileum in exchange for vitamin C and recycled back to the liver. Vitamin C is also absorbed in the ileum (1/3 in the jujenum, 1/3 in the ileum and 1/3 in the large intestine). Half of the fibre we consume is fermented in the large intestine producing gases which are partly responsible for our bowel movements. Also acts as a prebiotic stimulating the growth of Bifidobacteria and Lactobacillus. Probiotics are live microorganisms which when administered in adequate amounts confer a health benefit on the host - mainly used to treat diarrhoea (antibiotics often cause this as a side effect). Lactic acid produced by bacteria in the colon is also important for the maintenance of the epithelial barrier in the colon.  Some minerals are chelated (combined with organic molecules) in food and these need to be released before they can be absorbed. Phytate, found in cereals, legumes and grains, is a common chelator of Fe, Zn, Mg and Ca. These chelates are too big to pass through the enterocytes so the mineral is excreted. When we absorb phosphate the ligand exchange occurs and the mineral is released. Anything not absorbed goes out of the duodenum into the jejenum and then the large intestine.  I know this is long but it covers everything we've learnt about malabsorption and gives good examples of how nutrients get from the GI tract into the bloodstream. If you don't understand something ask! References: Kumar and Clark's Clinical Medicine; Dr Coffee's Case 11 lecture; NHS website; TJ's questions  All information has been taken from these sources and compiled into one document. I have tried to give credit wherever possible but if there is any plagiarism please let me know and I will take it down.
best_explanation: Calcium and iron are absorbed in the duodenum Glucose and bile salts are absorbed in the distal ileum (vitamin C and B12 are also absorbed in the ileum) Fructose is absorbed in the jejunum and duodenum (the majority in the jejunum)  Source: 'Food and the Gut' lecture in Case 11 'An Introduction to the Small and Large Bowel' PCS. instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: Which of the following would exacerbate the symptoms of Cushing’s disease? Option A: Taking glucocorticoids to treat asthma Option B: Taking a glucocorticoid receptor antagonist Option C: Somatic cells not responding to cortisol Option D: Radiation therapy to treat a pituitary adenoma The correct answer is Option A.
reference: Taking glucocorticoids to treat asthma - this will increase circulating cortisol levels and so exacerbate the symptoms of Cushing’s disease.  Taking a glucocorticoid receptor antagonist - this will reduce the effects of cortisol on target tissues, therefore exacerbating the symptoms of Cushing’s disease.  Somatic cells not responding to cortisol - cortisol normally has an effect on somatic cells via it’s receptor, the glucocorticoid receptor. In Cushing’s syndrome this receptor is down regulated or not activated by cortisol so this answer is irrelevant to the question.  Radiation therapy to treat a pituitary adenoma - this will damage the pituitary gland and decrease corticotropin release, therefore decreasing circulating cortisol levels and ameliorating the symptoms of Cushing’s disease.  SOURCE - Crash Course: Endocrine System. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U5ZgEHuI9eo&t=2s  plus personal experience of having had to take steroids for asthma and being told off for taking them with Cushing's disease!  (Also I made up the bit about radiation therapy so if that makes sense in hindsight please let me know)  Discussion -Cushing’s disease- due to hypersecretion of corticotropin from the pituitary glandCushing’s syndrome- due to increased levels of circulating cortisol (often due to tumour affecting the adrenal glands)There are some situations where cortisol levels may be elevated without it necessarily being Cushing’s syndrome or disease e.g. chronic stress or obesity but these were not mentioned in the options.  Ketoconazole (a type of antifungal medication) and dexamethasone (a synthetic steroid) are two examples of drugs which can be used to treat Cushing’s syndrome.  Source: http://endocrineweb.com/cushings/symptoms.html  https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/cushingstumor/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20353476   Also see lecture on the endocrine system in case 10.  Case 10 Coffey Lecture - Dr Alex Murray - Cushing's Disease, Addison's Disease & Acromegaly  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U5ZgEHuI9eo&t=2s   This is a really good lecture and worth a watch even if you don't have Cushing's disease!    Information from this video was used in answering this question.

Taking a glucocorticoid receptor antagonist would not exacerbate the symptoms of Cushing’s disease because the drug would block the effects of cortisol in the body.  Somatic cells not responding to cortisol would not exacerbate the symptoms of Cushing’s disease because the symptoms are due to HYPERsecretion of cortisol, not lack of response to cortisol.  Radiation therapy to treat a pituitary adenoma would exacerbate the symptoms of Cushing’s disease because it would DECREASE the amount of ACTH being released from the pituitary gland, resulting in less cortisol being released from the adrenal glands.  (Cushing’s disease is caused by high levels of cortisol circulating in the body.  Cushing’s syndrome can be caused by either high levels of cortisol circulating in the body or by increased ACTH being released from the pituitary gland, resulting in increased cortisol release from the adrenal glands.) input: Given question: Which part of the duodenum do would you find the common entrance for the bile and pancreatic ducts? Option A: Part 1 - Superior Option B: Part 2 - Descending Option C: Part 3 - Inferior Option D: Part 4 - Ascending Option E: None of the above The correct answer is Option B.
reference: 1) Sphincter of Oddi at the ampulla of Vater (hepatopancreatic sphincter) 2) Biliary duct and pancreatic duct join to form the hepato-pancreatic sphincter 3) CBD at 2 o'clock 4) Duodenal wall near the superior mesenteric artery (also has a branch of the coeliac trunk) Note: The sphincter of Oddi is also known as the hepatopancreatic sphincter. It lies at the ampulla of Vater and controls the entry of bile and pancreatic juice into the duodenum. It consists of smooth muscle (myenteric plexus) and has a large number of parasympathetic nerve endings. It contracts to prevent reflux of duodenal contents into the biliary and pancreatic ducts. It also contracts during digestion to slow the passage of food through the duodenum. Causes of pain in the sphinter of Oddi include: - blockage by a gallstone - inflammation due to cholecystitis or pancreatis - obstruction by a tumour  Symptoms of pain in the sphincter of Oddi include: - severe abdominal pain - vomiting - fever - jaundice - tender hepatomegaly - tenderness in the epigastrium - guarding - Rovsing's sign - lack of movement of bowels for several days - delayed gastric emptying - malabsorption - weight loss - anorexia - bloating - flatulence - belching - eructation - early satiety - nausea - vomiting - increased gas production - passage of gas and methane in urine - foul smelling gas passed rectally - fatty food intolerance - lactose intolerance - sorbitol intolerance - excessive gas formation after eating - bloating - abdominal distension - hard palmar crease (Budd's sign) - joint pain - bone spurs on x-ray imaging - diabetes - hypothyroidism - vitamin A deficiency - alopecia - seborrhoeic dermatitis - iron deficiency anaemia - peripheral neuropathy - adenoma - cancer Treatments for pain in the sphinter of Oddi include: - Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP): dye is injected into the bile and pancreatic ducts and X-rays are taken to see if there are any obstructions or blockages. If there is a blockage, a balloon catheter, bougie, or other device will be inserted to widen the duct. A stent may also be placed to keep the duct open. - Sphincterotomy: this involves cutting the sphincter of Oddi to improve flow through the duodenum. This is usually done during an ERCP procedure. Complications of sphincterotomy include: - bleeding - infection - pancreatic fistula - abscess - death - CBD stones - recurrent pancreatitis - accelerated pancreatic cancer - pseudocyst - abscess - fistula between two organs - haematemesis - melena - volvulus - cholangitis - liver abscess - biliary colics - acute pancreatitis - renal colic - Crohn's disease - ulcerative colitis - diverticular disease - appendicitis - cholecystitis - perforated peptic ulcer - gastrointestinal bleed - mesenteric ischaemia - bowel obstruction - hernias - anal fissures - Barrett's oesophagus - reflux disease - hiatal hernia - gastroparesis - intestinal failure - short bowel syndrome - malnutrition - vitamin deficiencies - osteoporosis - autoimmune diseases - IBD - cancer - dysmotility - gastrointestinal stromal tumours - lymphomas - thyroid cancer - adrenal cancer - gynaecological problems - urogynaecological procedures - menstrual disorders - endometriosis - pelvic floor dysfunction - interstitial cystitis - irritable bowel syndrome - restless legs syndrome - sleep disorders - headaches - neuralgias - chronic pain - fibrom
best_explanation: The common entrance for the bile and pancreatic ducts is the descending part of the duodenum (also the distal ileum).  The superior part of the duodenum is above the hepatis; the inferior part is below.  The ascending part is between the hepatis and duodenum, and the descending part is between the duodenum and jejunum.  The pancreas is found in the inferior part of the pancreatic tail, which is part of the descending duodenum.  The bile duct and pancreatic duct unite to form the duodenal papilla, which is the common opening for both ducts.  This opens onto the descending part of the duodenum.  SOURCE - Essential Clinical Anatomy, Prof. G.R.M. mutsaers, third edition, page 352. reference:
Central Nervous System = ectoderm  Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) = neuroderm  Epithelial linings of organs = endoderm  Connective tissue = mesoderm  Skin = ectoderm; hair, nails, sweat glands = neuroderm  Muscles = mesoderm  Blood and lymphatic vessels = adventitious (acrosome is a term often used interchangeably with adventitious, although technically inappropriately - see Case 14 lecture 'Blood Vessels'.)  Special senses = ectoderm  General senses = neuroderm  Epithelia of internal organs = endoderm  Gastric epithelium = entoderm  Respiratory epithelium = neuroderm  Urinary bladder epithelium = uroderm  Prostate = neuroderm  Mammary glands = neuroderm  Lining of the tubules in the kidney = nepro derm  Ciliated epithelium = neuroderm  Epithelium of the pharynx = neuroderm  Epithelium of the esophagus = neuroderm  Epithelium of the trachea = neuroderm  Epithelium of the bronchi = neuroderm  Epithelium of the lungs = neuroderm  Source: Essential Clinical Anatomy Lecture: "Approaches to Answering Questions" case 7. I found it helpful to draw a diagram with the three germ layers branching off from a central stem cell: Mesoderm --> Meso derivatives / connective tissue, muscle and blood/lymphatic vessel adventitious (acrosome) Ectoderm --> Ectoderm proper, CNS, PNS, special and general senses, EPITHELIAL LININGS OF ORGANS (this is important as it is often missed out), ciliated epithelium, lining of tubules in the kidney, respiratory epithelium, urinary bladder epithelium, prostate, mammary glands, lining of pharynx, trachea, bronchi and lungs. Endoderm --> Epithelial linings of organs, liver, pancreas, gastric epithelium, entoderm, epithelium of the urinary bladder, uroderm, prostate, mammary glands, pharynx, trachea, bronchi and lungs. Note: There are some discrepancies between different sources as to which germ layer gives rise to which structures. This table is based on the lecture in case 7, which appears to be consistent with most other sources. The table above shows the most commonly accepted answers, although there may be some variation. For example, in some sources the neural crest cells, which come from the ectoderm, are considered to contribute to the peripheral nervous system only, whereas others suggest they also contribute to the CNS. Similarly, there may be slight variations in which structures are considered to be derived from the mesoderm. However, the overall structure of the answer is likely to be similar. This table therefore provides a good starting point for answering questions about the composition of various structures. It should however be noted that this is a simplification of a more complex developmental process. Further reading: 'Early Human Development' plenary case 7. 'Before We Are Born' 6th Edition by Moore & Persaud. Pg.205-206. **Also, don't forget to check out the 'Coffey lecture' youtube video - it's really helpful in understanding this topic!**

input: Given question: You are a consultant cardiologist in Morriston hospital. A patient has come to see you for a follow up appointment to review their medication and progress after a recent myocardial infarction with ST elevation. They are a biochemistry lecturer and want to know all about the drugs they have been put on, particularly about Clopidogrel which they have not heard of before. How would you explain this drugs mechanism of action to your patient? Option A: It is an anti-platelet drug that inhibits the action of thrombin on platelets Option B: It is an anticoagulant that inhibits production of factor Xa. Option C: It is an anti-platelet drug that inhibits the production of factor Xa. Option D: It is an anti-platelet drug that prevents initiated platelets activating other platelets and starting a chain reaction. Option E: It is an anticoagulant that inhibits the production of fibrin. The correct answer is Option D.
reference:
Clopidogrel works by preventing initiated platelets activating other platelets and starting a chain reaction. This reduces the formation of thrombus in the vasculature.  A - Mechanism of action of Heparin B - Mechanism of action of Apixaban C - Mechanism of action of Dabigatran E - Mechanism of action of Rivaroxaban  Antiplatelet drugs are agents which prevent clotting of blood. They do so by inhibiting the action of thrombin on platelets. Thrombin is the enzyme that converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin. Fibrin is the main component of a thrombus (clot). Platelets stick to the fibrin of a thrombus and this traps them in position so that they cannot contribute to the further circulation of the blood. If enough platelets stick to a thrombus it will detach from the site of formation and move downstream. This can cause obstruction of a vessel and therefore interfere with the flow of blood. Antiplatelet drugs aim to reduce the risk of thrombosiso by inhibiting the action of thrombin on platelets. Thrombin inhibition results in reduced rate of thrombus formation. ADP (adenosine diphosphate) is released when a platelet reacts to damage to the endothelium or a clot associated protein. Increased concentration of ADP causes platelets to change shape so that they become more sticky (platelet aggregation). Aggregation causes the release of granules from the platelet and these contain clotting factors (as mentioned above). These factors are involved in the amplification cycle of clotting. Antiplatelet drugs also inhibit the aggregation of platelets. This is done by inhibiting the action of GpIIb/IIIa on the platelet. This is the same receptor that binds ADP and as such antiplatelet drugs also inhibit ADP binding. Aspirin is irreversibly bound to COX-1, a component of the cyclooxygenase enzyme. Cyclooxygenase catalyses the conversion of arachadonic acid to PGG2 via the unstable intermediate PGH2. PGH2 is the substrate for the synthesis of the prostacyclins, which are antiaggregatory for platelets and which also have an array of other effects including vasodilation, inhibition of leukotriene synthesis and inhibition of neutrophil migration. Prostacyclin synthesis is thus inhibited by aspirin. Aspirin is therefore an antiplatelet agent. Ticlopidine and Clopidogrel are also antiplatelet drugs. They inhibit the binding of ADP to its receptors on platelets. This prevents the early events in the process of platelet aggregation. Clopidogrel is a newer, more potent antiplatelet drug than ticlopidine. Clopidogrel is converted into its active metabolite by esterases. The active metabolite blocks the P2Y12 receptor on platelets. This prevents the early events in the process of platelet aggregation. Prasugrel is another antiplatelet drug that works by blocking the P2Y12 receptor, but it does so more quickly than clopidogrel. Prasugrel is only indicated in certain patients. All information has been taken from Dr Johnson's cardiovascular pharmacology lecture in case 13. I hope this helps! best_explanation: Clopidogrel is an anti-platelet drug that prevents initiated platelets activating other platelets and starting a chain reaction. It works by inhibiting the binding of adenosine diphosphate (ADP) to its platelet receptors.  This prevents the signal for the platelet to change shape and release granules which are pro-coagulant.  It is commonly used as an adjunct to aspirin in patients who have had an MI, particularly those with ST elevation. It is also used in patients undergoing PCI.  Its main side effect is that it can cause a bleed as it prevents the formation of fibrin.  It is an oral drug.  Adenosine diphosphate is a nucleoside diphosphate that acts as a cellular energy transfer molecule. It is used as an energy source by cells or as a signaling molecule.  It is released from the lymphocytes in response to IL1, IL6 or TNF.  It is also released from endothelial cells, mast cells, basophils, and platelets.  It is an important mediator of the inflammatory response.  When released from platelets it activates the GpIIb/IIIa receptor on the platelet which is involved in the platelet's haemostatic function.  When it binds to the GpIIb/IIIa receptor it causes the platelet to change shape and release granules which are pro-coagulant.  This is the main mechanism of action of Clopidogrel.  Aspirin works in a similar way but it inhibits the binding of adenosine diphosphate to its platelet receptors.  Thrombin inhibitors include S Coumarin (also an anti-coagulant) which inhibits the carboxylation of prothrombin to thrombin.  Anti-coagulants also include heparin which inactivates thrombin, and Warfarin which inhibits the synthesis of vitamin K dependent clotting factors.  Factor Xa inhibitors include Apixaban. Generally, the higher the level of injury the worse the functional outcome. However, this cannot be predicted by the degree of paralysis as some people may have good recovery despite a complete SCI while others may have little or no recovery despite a incomplete SCI. Factors that affect functional outcomes include: 1) Time since injury - early surgical intervention improves functional outcome. 2) Level and completeness of injury - high cervical and complete injuries tend to have a poorer functional outcome. 3) Age - younger individuals tend to have a better functional outcome. 4) General health - individuals who are generally fit and healthy prior to SCI tend to have a better functional outcome. 5) Rehabilitation - those who receive active rehabilitation tend to have a better functional outcome. 6) Psychological factors - depression, anxiety and stress can impair functional outcome. reference: 1. Down's - occurs in 1 in 600 pregnancies. Main signs and symptoms at birth are mental retardation, small head and hypotonia. Other defects include: cardiac defects, seizures, and craniofacial dysmorphism. 2. Patau (trisomy 13) - occurs in 1 in 6500 pregnancies. Main signs and symptoms at birth are severe developmental delay, microcephaly, holoprosencephaly, cyclopia and arthryogryposis. 3. Edward's - occurs in 1 in 500 pregnancies. Main signs and symptoms at birth are large tongue, small jaw, roof of mouth, heart, nose and middle ear malformations. 4. Turner's - occurs in 1 in 2000 pregnancies. Main signs and symptoms at birth are ambiguous genitalia, streak ovaries, primary amenorrhoea, lack of growth and development, and lack of sexual development at puberty. 5. Triplets, quadruplets and higher order multiples occur in 1 in 1000 pregnancies. Signs and symptoms depend on the number of foetuses, their birth weight and gestational age. Some possible outcomes include: prematurity, low birth weight, intrauterine growth restriction, macrosomatia and multiple birth syndromes. 6. Triploidy - occurs in 1 in 1000 pregnancies. Main sign is a small fetus with a large placenta. Other features may include: excess amniotic fluid, severe developmental delay, omphacele (organs outside body), and pottersequelosa (fused ribs). 7. XXY and XYY - occur in 1 in 1000 and 1 in 100 pregnancies respectively. Both have few clinical consequences. 8. Di George's - occurs in 1 in 5000 pregnancies. Characteristics include: cleft palate, congenital heart defects, short neck, low-set ears, failure of formation of thymus, and immune system problems. 9. Velocardiofacial - occurs in 1 in 5000 pregnancies. Main feature is a small chin. Other features may include: developmental delay, conduct disorders, and learning disabilities. 10. Silver-Russell - occurs in 1 in 10,000 pregnancies. Characteristics include: short stature, limb deficiencies, and facial abnormalities. Other possible features include: cleft palate, clubfeet, and low set ears. 11. Chromosomal mosaicism - occurs in 1 in 3 people. Features depend on which cells have trisomy, but it usually has no clinical consequences. input: Given question: You are examining a 38 year old female patient and find perpipheral signs including koilonychia, conjuctival pallor and angular stomatitis. When asked to state a possible cause of these signs you suggest... Option A: Apthous ulcers Option B: IBS Option C: Iron defficiency anaemia Option D: Oestrogen excess Option E: Pre-hepatic jaundice The correct answer is Option C.
reference: Koilonychia - spoon nails Angelual stomatitis - painful red tongue with sharp edges Conjunctival pallor - pale white sclera Irritability, fatigue, palpitations, shortness of breath, itching, joint pain before menstruation - classic symptoms of premenstrual syndrome (PMS). However in this case it may be due to iron deficiency as a cause of PMS. Explanation: Iron deficiency anaemia is a common cause of PMS symptoms. Iron is essential for the synthesis of brain neurotransmitters and also for myoglobin which takes iron to muscle cells to be used as part of the electron transport chain in mitochondria. Without enough iron, muscles become weak and tired, causing fatigue. Angle stomatitis is another sign of iron deficiency. As well as PMS symptoms, other common signs of low ferritin include being easily exhausted, headaches, dizziness, pale skin, slow wound healing and a fast or irregular heart rate. TREATMENT: Iron tablets will probably be prescribed. If you have any reason why you cannot take iron tablets then you should inform your doctor. For example, if you have a problem absorbing iron, have kidney disease, or are taking certain medications that interact with iron then your doctor might prescribe a different treatment. NICE guidelines recommend ferrous carbonate or ferrous sulfate as first line treatments. Iron tablets can cause constipation so your doctor might also prescribe a laxative. Also, avoid taking antacids at the same time as iron tablets because the iron will not be absorbed properly. Also, if you are a vegetarian or vegan, you should tell your doctor because you might need more iron than usual. Increasing your intake of foods high in vitamin C can also help iron absorption. Vitamin C can enhance the amount of iron that your body absorbs from your meals by up to five times. Foods rich in vitamin C include citrus fruits (such as oranges), berries, broccoli, bell peppers, and potatoes. Drinking tea or coffee with a meal can also decrease the amount of iron that you absorb. Limit your caffeine intake to see if this helps. It is important to follow up with your doctor to check your ferritin levels after starting iron treatment to make sure they are increasing. Source: 'Nutritional Anaemias' lecture in Case 10 and 'Iron Deficiency Anaemia' article on Patient.co.uk website. Other causes of PMS symptoms include pre-hepatic jaundice and excess oestrogen. best_explanation: Iron defficiency anaemia is characterised by koilonychia, conjunctival pallor and angular stomatitis. Other features include microcytic anaemia, dysphagia, dyspnoea, sore mucosae, pica and heart failure. The condition is rare in females of childbearing age as they are less likely to present with the classical symptoms of anaemia. A - apthous ulcers are painful, recurrent aphthous ulcers of the mouth B - IBS is a common cause of functional gastrointestinal disorders and has a prevalence of 10-15% in the general population. Other causes of these signs include chloride deficiency, cystic fibrosis, haemochromatosis, lymphoedema, myelodysplasia and thyroid dysfunction. Microcytic anaemia e.g. due to iron defficiency or thalassaemia, has a haemocrit below 33%.

input: Given question: Yvette is diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. Her diabetes nurse talks to her about some of the potential complications that can arise if her diabetes is poorly controlled. The nurse discusses different types of neuropathy, one of which is distal symmetrical polyneuropathy. Which of the following symptoms may suggest that a patient has this type of neuropathy? Option A: Diarrhoea and constipation Option B: Loss of vision Option C: Pain in the proximal leg with progression then partial recovery Option D: Postural hypotension Option E: Progressive loss of distal sensation The correct answer is Option E.
reference: Distal symmetrical polyneuropathy commonly presents with a progressive loss of distal sensation. It is the most common form of diabetic neuropathy. Other symptoms include paraesthesiae and pain in the feet. There are other forms of neuropathy including: * Proximal neuropathy - pain in the proximal leg with progression then partial recovery * Mononeuropathy - injury to a specific nerve e.g. carpal tunnel syndrome * Autonomic neuropathy - dysregulation of autonomic responses e.g. postural hypotension, gastroparesis, sexual dysfunction, bladder dysfunction This information was taken from the NICE guidelines on the treatment of type 2 diabetes. Source: Case 10, Plenary 2 - Understanding and managing diabetes as a chronic condition lecture - Dr R Sowden-Smith. For more information see: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg87/chapter/1-recommendations#initiating-and-monitoring-anti-diabetic-drug-treatment-including-insulin-1-3-and-their-combinations-to-achieve-targets-for-glucose-control-a-practical-approach-to-the-use-of-diabetes-drugs-including-insulin-in-clinical-practice-1-3-and-their-combinations-to-achieve-targets-for-glucose-control-a-practical-approach-to-the-use-of-diabetes-drugs-including-insulin-in-clinical-practice-9-2-and-9-3-mhra-guidance-on-the-use-of-medicines-in-patients-with-diabetes-5-complications-of-diabetes-1-3-and-their-management-1-3-and-their-management-1-3-and-their-management-1-3-and-their-management-mhra-guidance-on-the-use-of-medicines-in-patients-with-diabetes-appendix-a-definitions-of-some-terms-used-in-this-guide-3-3-and-their-management-1-3-and-their-management-mhra-guidance-on-the-use-of-medicines-in-patients-with-diabetes-appendix-a-definitions-of-some-terms-used-in-this-guide-3-3-and-their-management-1-3-and-their-management-mhra-guidance-on-the-use-of-medicines-in-patients-with-diabetes-appendix-a-definitions-of-some-terms-used-in-this-guide-3-3-and-their-management-1-3-and-their-management-mhra-guidance-on-the-use-of-medicines-in-patients-with-diabetes-appendix-a-definitions-of-some-terms-used-in-this-guide-3-3-and-their-management-1-3-and-their-management-mhra-guidance-on-the-use-of-medicines-in-patients-with-diabetes-appendix-a-definitions-of-some-terms-used-in-this-guide-3-3-and-their-management-1-3-and-their-management-mhra-guidance-on-the-use-of-medicines-in-patients-with-diabetes-appendix-a-definitions-of-some-terms-used-in-this-guide-3-3-and-their-management-1-3-and-their-management-mhra-guidance-on-the-use-of-medicines-in-patients-with-diabetes-appendix-a-definitions-of-some-terms-used-in-this-guide-3-3-and-their-management-1
