input: Given question: which would be indicative of WPW syndromw on an ECG? Option A: long PR intervals, delta wave Option B: short PR interval, bradycardia Option C: PR interval shortened, delta wave Option D: right axis deviation, long PR interval Option E: raised HR, theta wave The correct answer is Option C.
reference:
PR intervals are usually longer in women, so if a female patient has a short PR interval it is more likely to be bradycardia. However, in a male patient a short PR interval could indicate WPW syndrome. In this condition, there is an accessory pathway (the Bundle of Kent) present in the heart which allows impulses from the atria to bypass the AVN and go straight to the ventricles which causes a short PR interval. A delta wave is also usually present. If the accessory pathway was not present, then upon arrival of the impulse at the ventricles, a QRS complex would be recorded. RAD is when the axis of the heart is shifted to the right so that the top of the heart is depicted as being higher than the bottom. This will lengthen PR intervals. RAISED HR = theta waves THETA WAVES ARE USUALLY caused by fast discharge of adrenaline (epinephrine). They are steep and sharp and because they come after the P-wave, they indicate that the heart is contracting harder and faster. The AVN is the Atrioventricular node - this is where the electrical impulse must slow down as it goes from the atria to the ventricles. It is here that the pacemaker activity of the heart is normally regulated. BRADYKARDIA = slow heart rate ATRIAL FIBRILLATION = very rapid irregularly irregular heart action VENTRICULAR ARRYTHMIAS = originate in the ventricles, especially if caused by ischaemia. TACHYCARDIA = fast heart rates SINUS BRADYARRHYTHMIA = when the heart rate is too slow, usually less than 60 bpm. This is the most common arrhythmia and is usually caused by sick sinus syndrome. This is when the SA node fails to function properly. AF = atrial fibrillation - this is a type of tachyarrhythmia originating in the atria. It is a very irregular, often very fast heart rate. It is associated with failure of the AVN to control the heart rate so that the heart races away uncontrollably. Flutter = very rapid regular tachycardia (as compared to AF which is very fast and irregular). It is caused by the two competing pacemakers in the AV node. Wolf-Parkinson White Syndrome = accessory pathway between the atria and ventricles causes a short PR interval and a delta wave. It can lead to serious consequences such as sudden cardiac death. Wolff Parkinson White syndrome is one of the conditions that can cause a short PR interval. Other conditions that can do this include: hypothyroidism, anaemia, hypoxaemia, hyperkalaemia, digitalis intoxication and some drugs. It is important to note that a short PR interval can sometimes be normal in females. It is only if combined with other signs such as non-specific complaints or a history of palpitations that it should raise suspicion of Wolff Parkinson White syndrome. http://www.ecgpedia.org/index.php?title=PR_Interval http://www.heartrhythmalliance.org/our-work/education-and-awareness/arrhythmia-tutorials/basic-echocardiography-tutorial/normal-variants-of-the-ecg/ http://www.medical-institution.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/03/ECG-Interpretation.png [Note: I have tried to give an overview of the different types of ectopic rhythms and their characteristics. It is important to remember that ectopics can be very difficult to interpret and should be used in conjunction with changes in the baseline and other features to determine whether the ectopic is genuine or pathological.]

This is a condition where there is an accessory pathway, a bypass tract, which allows impulses from the SAN to bypass the AVN and go straight to the ventricles which causes a shortened PR interval and a delta wave. It can present with symptoms of palpitations and dizziness.  It is treated with ablation.  A VPC with 200J was delivered to the SAN in this case. The ECG shows right axis deviation and long PR interval.  B = 2nd degree AV block is when the PR interval is prolonged and there is a non-conducted p-wave. The ECG shows a long PR interval and no delta wave.  C = 1st degree AV block = normal 3rd degree AV block = no communication between atria and ventricles, no PR interval and no delta wave.  E = Wolf-Parkinson-White is a cause of a shortened PR interval and delta wave. It can present with symptoms of palpitations and dizziness. It is treated with ablation. VT is a cause of a non-conducted p-wave. It can present with symptoms of palpitations and syncope. It is treated with cardioversion.  This was covered in the case 15 wrap up.  I found this video really helpful in understanding the different types of AV blocks and the ECG findings http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6YiWdxx4kgs (accessed 17/12/2013) This was also covered in the case 15 wrap up.  Sources: Kumar and Clark, Dr Coffey's lectures.  I also found this website really helpful in understanding the different types of AV blocks and their causes and treatments http://www.heart.org/HEARTORG/Conditions/HeartRhythmDisorders/AVBLOCKS/Index.html (accessed 17/12/2013) Dr Coffey's ECG tutorial was also really helpful in understanding how to identify different ECG patterns.
